referee.strategy: Chronic-Fail Decay: systematically short (or avoid) cheap single names that appear on >=11 of the last ~13 semi-monthly SEC FTD prints, sized by price band, held ~2 weeks. Universe ~650-730 names/print, median price ~$1.93, dominated by optionable busted-growth names (PLUG, BYND, CGC, SPCE, HYZN, GETY, VUZI, LAES, VFS, FBIO).
referee.verdict: NO-EDGE (as a short strategy). The statistical pattern is real and was published a decade ago; the exploitable net-of-cost expectancy is negative with high confidence. The only surviving use is as a free long-side negative screen.
referee.edge_case: The pattern is real, is measured on a large clean sample (27.5M FTD rows, N=264,834 cohort observations), survives a matched control (fresh failers at identical prices are flat, 0.00%, in every band), survives the publication lag (median -0.21%), and is monotone in price — exactly the shape you would expect if it were an economic effect rather than noise: -1.92% ($0.5-1), -1.35% ($1-2), -0.95% ($2-3), -0.46% ($3-5), 0.00% ($5-10), +0.10% ($10-20). The market-neutral chronic-minus-fresh spread is negative in 13 of 17 years, so it is not one regime. It is independently corroborated in the literature: Stratmann & Welborn, "Informed short selling, fails-to-deliver, and abnormal returns," Journal of Empirical Finance 38 (2016) 81-102, finds stocks with FTDs earn negative abnormal returns proportional to their FTD levels, and that short sellers of high-FTD stocks earn positive estimated profits net of proprietary borrow-cost data. The economic mechanism is well-established: Miller (1977) overvaluation under binding short-sale constraints, empirically confirmed by Boehme, Danielsen & Sorescu, JFQA 41(2) 2006, 455-487, who find robust overvaluation specifically where high opinion dispersion AND short-sale constraints coexist — which is precisely the chronic-failer state. Finally, one cell of the cost stack does clear: PLUG at $2.26 with a verified 0.52% annualized borrow and 7.5M shares available (IB data via ChartExchange, 2026-08-12) costs ~0.02%/2wk to borrow plus ~0.44% tick-floor spread = ~0.46%, against a -0.95% band median. So the pattern is not fabricated and there exists at least one arithmetic configuration where gross beats cost.
referee.against_case:
Three independent kills, any one of which is fatal.

(1) THE MEAN IS POSITIVE. A fixed-dollar short book earns -mean(r), not -median(r). The analyst's own measurement: median -1.08% but MEAN +1.56%, p95 +21.8%, 3.96% of observations >+25%. An equal-weight short therefore loses ~1.56% per 2 weeks GROSS, ~-34%/yr arithmetic, before a single dollar of cost. You cannot harvest a median with a linear payoff. This is not a friction argument — the strategy has negative gross expectancy in its stated form.

(2) THE EDGE IS THE BORROW FEE, RE-DISCOVERED. Verified IB borrow rates (ChartExchange, 2026-08-12 21:22 EDT) are almost perfectly rank-correlated with the alleged edge, in the wrong direction for the trader: BYND $0.41 -> 35.87%; CGC $1.025 -> 12.30%; FBIO -> 8.27%; VUZI -> 2.98%; SPCE $3.30 -> 2.76%; PLUG $2.26 -> 0.52%. The cheap names that "decline" cost 12-36%/yr to borrow (0.47-1.38% per 2 weeks); the name that is cheap to borrow (PLUG, 0.52%) sits in the band where the edge is weakest and, critically, is NOT short-constrained at all (7.5M shares freely available), so the Miller/Boehme mechanism that supposedly generates the return does not apply to it. The fails themselves are a marker, not a flow — median fail notional $5,073 is economically nil.

(3) COSTS EXCEED THE LAG-HONEST EDGE BY 3-7x. The honest signal is -0.21% median, 45.0% hit rate. Minimum regulatory tick alone (SEC Rule 612: $0.01 for stocks >=$1.00, $0.005 only for names with TWA quoted spread <=$0.015, $0.0001 below $1.00) puts a hard floor of 0.44% (at $2.26) to 0.98% (at $1.025) on a single round trip against mid. Add 0.1-1.4%/2wk borrow. The cost floor is 0.5-1.5% per 2 weeks against a 0.21% signal.

Supporting: the chronic-failer state is directly observable in real time via borrow fee, utilization, short interest, and the Reg SHO threshold list (published DAILY by Nasdaq/NYSE/Cboe). The FTD print is a noisy, 2-6 week stale, lower-resolution proxy for a variable anyone can see live and that is already reflected in the lending market's price.
referee.who_is_on_other_side:
1) THE SHARE LENDER — the dominant counterparty and the one who is unambiguously right. Whoever lends BYND collects 35.87%/yr or CGC 12.30%/yr on a daily-marked, over-collateralized, effectively riskless loan. That is the actual return stream this strategy has discovered, and the lender, not the shorter, receives it. Drechsler & Drechsler's shorting premium (NBER w20282) is precisely this: the cheap-minus-expensive-to-short portfolio earns 1.43%/mo gross but 0.91% net, i.e. ~36% of the gross is handed straight to lenders, and the residual is compensation for concentrated short risk borne by the few investors who do the shorting.

2) THE OPTIONS MARKET MAKER. Hard-to-borrow status depresses the synthetic forward via put-call parity, so puts are bid up and calls marked down mechanically. The MM sells you an already-borrow-adjusted put at very high IV (BYND IV reported at 234% — single-sourced, treat as indicative) and delta-hedges. They are indifferent to drift; they are selling you the borrow you were trying to avoid paying, plus a variance margin.

3) THE LOTTERY BUYER. Retail buyers of $0.41 stocks are knowingly paying for right-skew (Bali, Cakici & Whitelaw, JFE 99 (2011) 427-446). They accept a negative median in exchange for the +596% tail. They are rational under prospect theory and they are the reason the median is negative and the mean is positive at the same time. Shorting them means selling lottery tickets — a real risk premium, not an inefficiency.

4) THE INCUMBENT SHORTS, and this is the one that hurts. The boat is already full. BYND short interest reportedly reached ~82% (secondary sources; I could not independently verify the float-percentage figure — shortinteresttracker returned 403). Only 95,000 shares of BYND remain borrowable at IB. You are not adding information; you are the marginal 100,001st share in a maximally crowded trade, taking the squeeze risk that the earlier shorts have already de-risked.

- Sub-$1 ($0.0001 increments allowed): quoting is finer but realized spreads on a $0.41 Nasdaq name run ~$0.0025-$0.01 = 0.6-2.4%

COMMISSIONS: ~$0.0035/share IB. On a $1.00 stock that is 0.35% per side, 0.70% round trip — commissions on penny-priced stocks are charged per share, so they are catastrophic at low prices. Capped tiers help but this remains 0.1-0.7%.

MARGIN / CAPITAL DRAG: FINRA Rule 4210 maintenance for shorts below $5 is $2.50/share OR 100% of market value, whichever is greater. Shorting BYND at $0.41 ties up $2.50/share = 610% of notional. Return on required capital is divided by ~6 in the exact price band ($0.5-1) where the edge is largest. Above $5 the requirement is $5.00/share or 30% — but the edge is 0.00% there.

SHORT REBATE FORGONE: effective fed funds 3.63% (Aug 2026). IBKR pays short-proceeds interest only pro-rated below $100k NAV, so a small trader forgoes most of ~3.6%/yr = ~0.14%/2wk versus an institution.

OPTIONS ROUTE: does not rescue it. Penny Interval Program tick is $0.01 below $3.00 premium; a 2-week ATM put on a $1.35 stock at 150% IV is worth roughly $0.16, so a realistic $0.02-0.05 quoted width is 12-30% of premium round trip against a target edge worth ~$0.018 (1.35% of spot). At BYND's reported 234% IV the 2-week sigma is ~46% of spot and an ATM put costs ~18% of spot. And the borrow is already inside the price: as Nasdaq's own guidance states, when a stock becomes hard-to-borrow "option premiums will go up in put markets and go down in call markets, effectively limiting the advantage gained by synthesizing the short position."

TAX: 2-week holds are 100% short-term ordinary income; substitute payments in lieu received on the long leg of any pair are non-qualified. Assume a 25-45% haircut on any surviving gross.

TOTAL REALISTIC COST STACK: 1.2-2.5% per 2 weeks, i.e. 31-65% annualized at 26 turns/yr.
referee.capacity:
Binding constraint is borrow availability, not capital, and it is brutally small in exactly the names that carry the signal. Verified shares available at IB (2026-08-12): BYND 95,000 shares = ~$39k of borrowable notional; CGC 250,000 = ~$256k; FBIO 300,000; VUZI 200,000; SPCE 2,100,000 = ~$6.9M; PLUG 7,500,000 = ~$17M. Note the inversion: the two names with real borrow depth (PLUG, SPCE) are the two with negligible borrow fees and therefore no short-constraint mechanism and the weakest band edges.

PER TRADE: In the $0.5-2 band where the edge lives, realistic per-name size is the lesser of (a) ~50% of IB's displayed borrow, and (b) 5% of ADV over a 1-2 day entry. CGC is the LIQUID end of this universe (ADV 7.79M shares, ~$8M/day) and still only offers ~$256k of borrow. The median universe name at $1.93 with a few hundred thousand shares of ADV supports $20-80k. Call it $30-80k per name, and $250k as a hard ceiling in the most liquid names.

PORTFOLIO: you need 60-150 names to diversify a distribution with p95 of +21.8% and a 3.96% tail above +25%. At $30-80k each: $2-8M gross short is the honest ceiling, and the upper half of that range is only reachable by pushing into the illiquid tail where spread and impact are worst. I would put the practical ceiling at $3-5M gross for a book that is not immediately impact-dominated.

PER YEAR: 26 turns at $3-5M gross = $80-130M of traded notional annually, and every dollar of it crosses a 0.5-1.0% tick-floor spread plus impact. Turnover cost alone runs $1.5-4M/yr against a gross signal that, on the mean, is negative.

FOR A SMALL TRADER SPECIFICALLY: the fixed cost stack (spread, borrow, per-share commission, 4210 margin) is IDENTICAL at $50k of capital as at $5M — it is percentage-of-notional, not dollar-fixed. Being small does not help here; it hurts, because sub-$100k accounts also forgo the short rebate and cannot diversify across enough names to make the median rather than the tail dominate. There is no "too small to matter" regime for this trade.
referee.decay_evidence:
PUBLISHED TEN YEARS AGO ON THE SAME DATASET. Stratmann & Welborn, "Informed short selling, fails-to-deliver, and abnormal returns," Journal of Empirical Finance 38 (2016) 81-102, using SEC FTD data, already reports that FTD stocks earn negative abnormal returns proportional to FTD levels and that short sellers of high-FTD stocks profit net of borrow costs. This is not a new discovery. McLean & Pontiff (2016) document that post-publication anomaly returns are ~50% smaller; the analyst's own lag-honest -0.21% versus in-print -1.08% is consistent with exactly that decay having already occurred.

THE DECISIVE PAPER. Muravyev, Pearson & Pollet, "Anomalies and Their Short-Sale Costs," Journal of Finance 80(6), 2025: across 162 anomalies the average long-short return is +0.14%/month gross but -0.01%/month after short-sale costs; and the anomalies are not profitable EVEN BEFORE FEES once the high-fee observations (12% of stock-dates) are excluded. The chronic-fail cohort IS that 12%. This paper is the general theorem of which the present strategy is a specific instance, and it is largely out-of-sample relative to the original anomaly publications.

THE PREMIUM WAS ALREADY NAMED AND PRICED. Drechsler & Drechsler (NBER w20282) show the cheap-minus-expensive-to-short spread earns 1.43%/mo gross, 0.91% net, with the highest-fee decile costing 5.8%/yr and the top 5% costing 9.1%/yr, and that eight major anomalies "effectively disappear within the 80% of stocks that have low short fees" while being amplified only among high-fee names. A Fama-French + CME factor model largely spans them. In factor language, this strategy is short CME, short lottery/MAX, short junk. Those are priced factors sold as index products, not alpha.

COMMERCIALIZED AND FREE. The raw data is a free SEC download. The screen is trivially reproducible. Vendors already package it: ForcedAlpha runs a "Failure-to-Deliver Tracker — SEC FTD Data by Ticker," OptionsAnalysisSuite publishes documentation teaching traders to read "persistent FTDs (especially threshold-list status)" as a hard-to-borrow signal and to price synthetic-stock strategies against borrow rebates, and ChartExchange/Fintel/ORTEX/ShortInterestTracker all sell the higher-resolution real-time version (borrow fee, utilization, short interest). Worse, the underlying state is published DAILY and free: the Reg SHO threshold securities list (fails >=10,000 shares and >=0.5% of shares outstanding for 5 consecutive settlement days) is disseminated by Nasdaq, NYSE and Cboe every day, with no 2-6 week lag.

THE TAIL IS ALIVE AND RECENT, NOT HISTORICAL. BYND ran from $0.52 to $3.62 on closing prices between Oct 16 and Oct 21, 2025 — +596% in four trading days, in a sub-$1 chronic failer. Contemporaneous analysis attributes it primarily to social-media meme flow rather than a pure squeeze, which is worse for you: the tail is driven by an exogenous process you cannot forecast or fade. SPCE's 52-week range as of Aug 2026 is $2.13-$8.90 (318%). In April 2026 Avis (CAR) squeezed on a Pentwater stake build to 22% and then imploded 72% in 26 hours. This regime is not decaying — the meme/lottery bid that generates the +1.56% mean is structurally present in 2025-26.

SURVIVORSHIP CHURN IS CONFIRMED, NOT THEORETICAL. HYZN was delisted from Nasdaq on Jan 30, 2025 and deregistered under a Plan of Dissolution. BYND received a Nasdaq bid-price deficiency notice on Mar 4, 2026 and executed a 1-for-30 reverse split effective Aug 13, 2026. Nasdaq tightened the rules effective Jan 17, 2025 (suspension after 360 days of non-compliance, down from 540; immediate delisting determination with no grace period if a company falls below $1 within a year of a reverse split). 121 Nasdaq/NYSE delistings and 158 bid-price deficiency notices by Apr 21, 2025; 145 reverse splits by that date; 495 reverse splits in 2023. This validates the 51% two-year churn — and every one of those events is a forced buy-in, a non-standard option deliverable, or an untradeable OTC stub for a short book.
referee.net_edge_estimate:
Per 2-week period, short side, at the cohort-realistic center of the universe (~$1.93 median price, 8-20%/yr borrow, $0.01 tick):

ON THE MEDIAN, LOOKAHEAD (the number the backtest shows): +1.35% gross (as a short, $1-2 band) - 0.74% spread - 0.46% borrow - 0.10% commission = -0.05%/2wk. Zero, before slippage. Even the most flattering cell available, PLUG-like ($2-3, 0.52% borrow, $0.44% spread), nets ~+0.49%/2wk = ~+13%/yr gross of slippage and tax — and that cell is precisely the one with cheap, abundant borrow, i.e. no short constraint, i.e. no mechanism.

ON THE MEDIAN, LAG-HONEST (the only tradeable number): +0.21% gross - 1.20 to 2.50% cost = -1.0% to -2.3% per 2 weeks = -26% to -60% annualized. Decisively negative.

ON THE MEAN, WHICH IS WHAT A FIXED-DOLLAR SHORT ACTUALLY EARNS: -1.56% gross - 1.20 to 2.50% cost = -2.8% to -4.1% per 2 weeks = -52% to -66% annualized, with a fat left tail from the 3.96% of names that run >+25% and the occasional BYND that runs +596% in four days. A 60-name book with a 4% chance per name per fortnight of a >25% adverse move expects ~2.4 such events every two weeks; sizing that keeps any single +596% event from being terminal forces per-name notional so small that fixed per-share commissions dominate.

I want to be explicit about what is and is not knowable. The gross pattern is measured, not estimated — I take the analyst's -1.08% median / +1.56% mean / -0.21% lag-honest at face value. The borrow rates are verified point-in-time observations from IB for six named stocks on one date; I could NOT obtain historical borrow time series (paywalled) or the cohort-wide borrow distribution, so the 8-20%/yr cohort assumption is my inference from the six observations plus Drechsler's decile structure and should be treated as uncertain to roughly +/-8 points. I could NOT obtain live NBBO spreads — my spread numbers are Rule 612 tick floors, which are lower bounds; true costs are higher. The 234% BYND IV is single-sourced and indicative only.

None of that uncertainty matters to the conclusion, because the decisive facts are not the ones I estimated. The mean being +1.56% comes from the analyst's own 264,834-observation measurement and kills a linear short outright. The lag-honest median being -0.21% against a tick-size floor of 0.44-0.98% is arithmetic on a regulatory constant. Even if every borrow fee were zero, the trade would still lose.

WHAT SURVIVES: as a long-side negative screen, the chronic-fail flag is free — no borrow fee, no squeeze exposure, no 4210 margin charge, no forced buy-in — and the 51% two-year delisting/reverse-split churn plus verified Nasdaq rule tightening give it a solid prior. Excluding chronic failers priced under $5 from a long book is, in my judgment, a genuinely sensible risk control, though its measured benefit (avoiding a -1% median) is well inside the noise of most long portfolios and should not be oversold as alpha.
referee.confidence:
HIGH that no exploitable short edge exists; MEDIUM-HIGH on the precise magnitude of the loss.

Reasons for high confidence: (1) The two decisive numbers come from the commissioning analyst's own data, not from my research — a +1.56% mean and a -0.21% lag-honest median. A fixed-dollar short earns the negative of the mean; that is arithmetic, not opinion, and it means the strategy has negative expectancy BEFORE any cost I researched. (2) The spread floor is a regulatory constant (SEC Rule 612: $0.01 above $1.00, $0.005 only for demonstrably tight names) and at a $1.93 median price it is 0.52% per round trip, more than double the honest signal. (3) Borrow rates are verified primary-source observations from Interactive Brokers for six of the ten named chronic stocks, and they are inversely aligned with the edge in exactly the way Muravyev-Pearson-Pollet predict. (4) The result is already published (Stratmann & Welborn 2016, same dataset), already factor-spanned (Drechsler CME factor, Bali MAX, Asness QMJ), already commercialized by multiple vendors, and the underlying state is disseminated free and daily via the Reg SHO threshold list. (5) The JF 2025 paper is a direct, out-of-sample, general refutation: 162 anomalies go from +0.14%/mo gross to -0.01%/mo net of borrow, and are unprofitable even gross once the high-fee 12% is removed. This strategy is entirely inside that high-fee 12%. (6) Three independent kill mechanisms — negative gross mean, cost floor exceeding the signal, and the edge being the borrow fee itself — each sufficient alone; all three would have to be wrong simultaneously.

Reasons the magnitude estimate is only medium-high: I could not obtain live NBBO spreads (used tick-size floors, which understate cost), could not obtain historical or cohort-wide borrow distributions (six point observations plus literature deciles), could not verify BYND's current short-interest percentage of float (source returned 403), and the 234% IV figure is single-sourced. Every one of these gaps, if resolved, makes the trade WORSE, not better — my estimate is biased in the strategy's favor and it still fails.

The single most important thing I would tell the analyst: you did not discover an FTD anomaly, you rediscovered the securities-lending fee. The signal ranks names by how expensive they are to borrow, and the lender charges you the entire spread. If you want to test whether anything is left, do not run a short book — measure the MEAN (not the median) of the market-neutral chronic-minus-fresh spread, and regress the chronic-minus-fresh return on the contemporaneous borrow fee. If the alpha vanishes when you control for the fee, which I expect, the question is closed.

referee.strategy: Reg SHO Threshold-List Overvaluation Reversal — short (or buy puts on) names newly added to / persisting on SRO Reg SHO threshold lists, per Autore, Boulton & Braga-Alves (2015), Financial Review 50(2), 143-172.
referee.edge_case:
The gross statistical pattern is real, large, and I verified it independently — it is not a data artifact.

I downloaded 879 daily Nasdaq Reg SHO threshold lists (2023-01-03 to 2026-08-11, 34,284 name-days) and joined them to the analyst's 27M-row SEC FTD panel for prices. Common stock only (ETPs/warrants/units stripped), 21-trading-day horizon, short-side returns:

- PERSISTING on list (>=18 of prior 20 days): N=3,441, median +20.3%, mean +12.3%, 75.9% of observations declined.
- NEW ADDITIONS: N=1,506, median +13.3%, 67.9% declined.
- By price: <$2 median +21.3%; $2-5 +21.8%; $5-20 +20.5%.

It survives the checks that killed the naive FTD-spike signal:
1. NO LOOK-AHEAD. Entry-lag sensitivity is flat — 21d median short return is +20.0% at lag 0, +19.8% at lag 1, +19.6% at lag 2, +19.5% at lag 3, +19.0% at lag 5, +17.4% at lag 10. The threshold list is published free and real-time by the SRO (unlike the ~1-month-lagged FTD file), so the signal is genuinely actionable.
2. MATCHED CONTROL. Against chronic-FTD failers that never touched the list, same price band, same dates: control 21d median ~0.0% to -2.6% vs threshold-persist +20-22%. Spread of -19 to -21pp.
3. INCREMENTAL to the analyst's existing chronic-fail signal. Within the chronic-fail + price<$5 cohort: on-list 21d median short +18.8% (N=1,412) vs not-on-list +4.0% (N=121,336). Incremental +14.8pp median / +9.3pp mean. Only 51% of threshold-persist name-days are even captured by the chronic-fail flag, so this is a distinct, additive signal.
4. STABLE ACROSS YEARS. Gross 21d median short return: 2023 +10.3%, 2024 +19.0%, 2025 +21.5%, 2026 +24.2% — strengthening, not decaying.

referee.against_case:
Four independent kill shots, any one of which is sufficient.

1. IT IS NOT THE PAPER'S EFFECT. Autore et al. sampled 2005-2008 — entirely pre-Rule 204 (interim 204T Sept 2008, permanent July 2009), which imposed T+4 close-out on ALL equities and cut fails 63.4% overall and 80.5% for threshold stocks (SEC OEA memo, Nov 2009). The regime studied no longer exists. More damning: their mechanism is overvaluation-then-reversal, which requires a run-UP first. In 2023-2026 the pre-event drift is strongly NEGATIVE — threshold names are down a median 18.8% (new adds) to 29.4% (persisters) over t-63 to t-21 before they ever hit the list, and down another 5.8-16.8% over t-21 to t-5. These are names already in free-fall that keep falling. That is toxic-convertible/ATM dilution CONTINUATION, not overvaluation REVERSAL. The paper's label is on the wrong phenomenon.

2. THE LIST HAS BEEN COLONIZED BY LEVERAGED ETPs. Of the 74 names on the 2026-08-11 Nasdaq list: 36 common stock, 34 ETPs, 4 warrants. The most persistent members across 20 monthly snapshots are all single-stock leveraged/inverse ETFs (SMCX 16/20, SMST 15/20, IONZ 14/20, MSTX 12/20, HIMZ 12/20, PLTZ 11/20, OKLL 11/20). US single-stock levered ETFs did not exist until July 2022 — they cannot have been in the 2005-08 sample. Their fails are mechanical creation/redemption artifacts. Shorting them LOSES: ETP-only 21d median short +8.4% but mean -3.8%. The list grew from ~20 names (2023) to ~67 (2026) almost entirely on this structural noise.

3. THE COST STACK EXCEEDS THE GROSS EDGE BY 3x. See frictions — 8 of the 20 highest-borrow-fee stocks in the entire US market are on today's threshold list, at 756-1,074%/yr.

4. THE PORTFOLIO SHARPE IS ZERO. On the only plausibly-borrowable subset (price>=$5), equal-weight, netting only a generous 3% round-trip and 60%/yr borrow: mean +2.14% per 21 days but standard deviation 32.5%, t-statistic 0.46 on ~47 independent monthly observations. Worst portfolio 21-day outcome: -146.5%. The "huge median" is an illusion created by holding 1-5 names at a time with a catastrophic left tail: P(single short loses >50% in 21d) = 4.4%, P(loses >100%) = 1.9%, worst individual outcomes -403%, -414%, -439%.
referee.who_is_on_other_side:
Four counterparties, each rationally and profitably.

1. SECURITIES LENDERS (the real winners). They collect 756-1,074%/yr on these exact names with zero price risk and a daily recall option. They are monetizing the entire anomaly as a lending rent, not a return. Any small trader shorting is simply paying that rent to them.

2. TOXIC-CONVERTIBLE / ATM FINANCIERS. Death-spiral convertibles use floating conversion prices at 20-50% discounts to a lookback average; the holder shorts against shares not yet delivered — which is precisely what generates the fails-to-deliver that put the name on the list. They are already short at a structurally guaranteed profit and need no borrow (they deliver into conversion). They will always out-execute you and they are the direct cause of the price decline you are trying to capture.

3. RETAIL SQUEEZE-HUNTERS. The dominant retail reading of the threshold list is BULLISH — the "T+13 forced covering" narrative (widely circulated on TradingView, Fintel, shortsqueeze.com, meme forums) says threshold inclusion forces shorts to buy in. They are the marginal buyer, and they are the reason the trade works 70-76% of the time. But they are also the reason it blows up: they periodically win enormously (HTZ was +14.3% on the day I sampled it, on $195M of volume). You are selling lottery tickets to a crowd that occasionally hits.

4. OPTIONS MARKET MAKERS. They sell you puts at 123-797% implied volatility with 20-83%-wide markets and are compensated for the pin/halt/gap risk they cannot hedge (they cannot borrow the underlying either). Their put prices already embed the full historical decline — see net_edge_estimate.

referee.decay_evidence:
FULLY COMMERCIALIZED AND FREE — there is no information advantage of any kind.

The threshold lists are published daily, free, in real time, by every venue: Nasdaq (nasdaqtrader.com/dynamic/symdir/regsho/, which is where I pulled 879 daily files in minutes), NYSE, Cboe (cboe.com/us/equities/market_statistics/reg_sho_threshold/), FINRA for OTC (otce.finra.org/otce/RegSHOThreshold/archives), and OTC Markets. Fintel flags every threshold name with a "T" marker in its short-squeeze screener and maintains a dedicated Reg SHO topic page. shortsqueeze.com publishes the list as a standalone product. Ortex, chartexchange and TradingView all surface it. Any signal available free from the primary regulator, redistributed by at least five vendors, and with an active retail following is not a source of alpha.

WHO ALREADY TRADES IT: securities lending desks (who capture the entire economics as a fee, risk-free), toxic-convertible and ATM financiers (who are structurally short via conversion rights and need no borrow), and options market makers (who price it at 123-797% IV). The professionals monetizing this phenomenon are not taking directional risk at all — they are renting scarcity. That is the tell that the "return" is a lending rent, not an anomaly.

HAS THE PATTERN ITSELF DECAYED? Honestly, no — the GROSS pattern has strengthened (2023 +10.3% -> 2026 +24.2% median 21d short return). But this is not evidence of surviving alpha; it is evidence that the cost of shorting has risen in lockstep. Acadian documents that the share of the US market costing more than 1% to borrow rose from under 10% in 2001 to about 50% in 2023. The gross spread widened because the borrow rent widened. The residual to a fee-payer has not improved.

WHAT HAS DECAYED IS THE SIGNAL'S MEANING. Post-Rule 204 the list stopped being a "persistent naked-short overvaluation" indicator and became (a) a leveraged-ETP creation/redemption artifact register — 34 of 74 current names — and (b) a roster of the market's most expensive borrows. Neither is tradeable.

CROWDED — BUT ON THE WRONG SIDE. The dominant retail narrative reads threshold inclusion as bullish "T+13 forced covering." That crowding is what makes the short work 76% of the time and what makes it lose 100-440% the other 4%.

referee.confidence:
HIGH that there is no exploitable net edge for a small trader or small fund. Medium-high on the precise magnitude of the gross pattern.

WHY HIGH: the conclusion does not rest on the return estimate at all. It rests on two independently verified facts that cannot be argued around. First, 8 of the 20 highest-borrow-fee stocks in the entire US market sit on today's 74-name threshold list at 756-1,074%/yr — a 31x concentration versus random — which means a 30-day hold costs 63-88% of notional against a 19-21% gross median. Second, the most liquid optionable name on the list, HTZ, prices a 22-day ATM put at 20.2% of spot against a 20.3% median 21-day decline, i.e. the options market has already fully priced the effect. Both are direct measurements from live market data taken today, not estimates. Additionally the paper's own authors state the mispricing "is likely to be difficult to arbitrage because of extreme shorting costs" — they never claimed it was tradeable.

WHY NOT HIGHER ON THE GROSS MAGNITUDE — things I could NOT verify, stated plainly:
- The IBKR borrow fees came from chartexchange's screener with NO visible timestamp. I could not reach IBKR's own securities-lending file from this environment (both the FTP and https endpoints returned nothing). The 8/20 overlap is so extreme it is robust to staleness, but treat the individual percentages as indicative rather than executable quotes.
- Cboe quotes were captured after the close (last trade 2026-08-12 16:00), so spreads may be wider than mid-session. I have flagged them as an upper bound; intraday spreads on the common names are likely somewhat tighter than the 4.28% median.
- Put-call-parity implied borrow assumes European-style parity on American options with no dividends. Early exercise on hard-to-borrow names biases this; treat 25-88%/yr as an order-of-magnitude estimate.
- I used ONLY the Nasdaq threshold list. NYSE, Cboe and the FINRA OTC lists are not included; the OTC list in particular is larger and would be strictly worse on every friction.
- I have no shares-outstanding data, so I could not reconstruct threshold membership before 2023-01-03. The 3.5-year window covers 879 trading days and ~47 independent monthly observations — adequate but not long.
- Prices are the FTD file's embedded prior-day closes, unadjusted for splits. I applied a +/-70% one-day guard at entry, but reverse splits inside the forward window remain and bias short returns DOWNWARD (making my gross figures conservative).
- Returns condition on the name reappearing in the FTD file later. Delistings-to-zero drop out, which biases short returns DOWNWARD too. So the true gross is if anything better than I report — and the net conclusion is unaffected, because the borrow fee is 3x the gross either way.

RECOMMENDATION: reject as a trade. Adopt the on-threshold-list flag as a free do-not-own screen alongside the existing chronic-FTD filter, and route the research effort elsewhere. If anyone wants exposure to this phenomenon, the economically correct expression is to be the LENDER, not the short — but that requires a prime brokerage balance sheet, not a trading account.

referee.strategy: FTD-Confirmed Short-Constraint Long-Short — use SEC fails-to-deliver (chronic-persistence + low-price pattern) as a confirming filter on a high-borrow-fee / high-utilization / high-days-to-cover short-constraint anomaly, traded by a small trader or small fund.
referee.edge_case:
The strongest honest case has four legs.

(1) The underlying median effect is real and survives my correction. Re-running the analyst's own panel (/home/user/WireAntennaGain/research/data/ftd/parquet/ftd_all.parquet, 27.5M rows) with a horizon-matched forward return applied identically to both groups, chronic failers (>=80 fail-days/180d) in cheap bands still show negative median 2-week returns: -2.02% ($0.50-1), -1.35% ($1-2), -1.04% ($2-3), -0.64% ($3-5), decaying to -0.11% ($5-10) and ~0 above $10. The dose-response in the median is monotonic (p180 0-20: 0.00%; 20-40: -0.45%; 40-60: -1.03%; 60-80: -1.27%; 80-100: -1.27%). This is a genuine, large-sample (n>1M) statistical regularity, not noise.

(2) Short-constraint variables genuinely predict negative returns in top-tier literature. Muravyev/Pearson/Pollet (JFE 2025) find fees, utilization, days-to-cover and fee risk all predict negative abnormal returns.

(3) Drechsler & Drechsler (NBER w20282) is the single best pro-edge citation: their cheap-minus-expensive-to-short portfolio earned 1.31%/month gross and, critically, 0.78%/month NET of lending fees with a 1.44% four-factor alpha — i.e. a published claim that the shorting premium survives its own borrow cost. Anomalies "effectively disappear within the 80% of stocks that have low short fees but are greatly amplified among those with high fees," which is exactly the conditioning this strategy proposes.

(4) The zero-cost version is genuinely valuable: as a negative screen — never go long a sub-$5 stock that fails on most trading days — the pattern is robust, free to apply, and no friction can eat it. That use survives everything below.
referee.against_case:
The case against is decisive on three independent levels.

(1) THE FTD SIGNAL AS REPORTED IS A FILTER ARTIFACT. I reproduced the analyst's headline cell exactly (N=23,203, median -1.8036%, mean -0.4719%, 58.26% down) and then found the cause. Line 46 of /home/user/WireAntennaGain/research/data/ftd/analyze_patterns.py defines the forward return as `CASE WHEN datediff('day',dt,d1) BETWEEN 7 AND 35 THEN p1/price-1`, where d1 is the next same-symbol row. But a chronic failer by construction appears on the file almost every day: of 1,020,046 chronic rows in the $0.50-5 band, 63.4% have a 1-day gap, 23.2% a 2-3 day gap, 11.1% a 4-6 day gap — and only 2.27% fall in the 7-35 day window. The reported result is computed on 2.27% of the cohort, selected precisely on the condition that the name's daily fail streak broke for 1-5 weeks and then RESUMED. That conditions on a future event (reappearing on the file), and reappearance is itself driven by renewed short pressure. The control group is not filtered the same way: occasional names (p180<=20) naturally have gaps >7 days, so essentially all their rows survive. The comparison is between two differently-selected populations. Using the actual next observation (gap 1-35d, 99.9% of chronic rows), the same cell gives median +0.000%, mean +1.083%, 49.2% down — no effect at all.

(2) THE MEAN — THE ONLY STATISTIC A PORTFOLIO EARNS — IS THE WRONG SIGN, AND IS NOT EVEN SIGN-IDENTIFIABLE. On the horizon-matched panel, chronic $0.50-5 has median -1.16% but mean +7.29% (n=1,013,480). A short book earns the negative of the mean, so equal-weight shorting loses. Worse, the sign flips on an arbitrary trimming choice affecting under 0.6% of observations: trimming forward ratios >1.8x leaves mean -1.02% (short earns +1.02%); >3x leaves -0.61%; >5x leaves -0.34%; >10x leaves +0.19% (short LOSES); >25x leaves +0.83% (short loses more). The q0.999 return is +615%, q0.9999 is +2,168%, max +899,900%. Because the FTD file's embedded prices are unadjusted prior-day closes, these extremes are an unseparable mix of genuine squeezes (catastrophic for a short) and reverse splits (neutral for a short, since you are adjusted). Chronic-fail sub-$5 microcaps are exactly the population that reverse-splits constantly. The gross expectancy of this trade therefore cannot be determined from this dataset at all — which by itself disqualifies it from a book.

(3) EVEN GRANTING THE MOST FAVORABLE GROSS NUMBER, BORROW ALONE IS ~2x THE EDGE. The best-case trim gives +1.02% per 2-week cycle (~30%/yr gross compounded). A 50%/yr borrow fee — mid-range for these names — costs 1.92% over 14 days. Borrow fee alone is roughly double the entire most-favorably-measured gross edge, before spread, commission, or margin.

(4) FTD ADDS NO INCREMENTAL INFORMATION. It is mechanically downstream of borrow cost, not independent of it. Evans/Geczy/Musto/Reed (RFS 2009, "Failure Is an Option") show that option market makers, who may short without borrowing, in most hard-to-borrow situations CHOOSE not to borrow and instead fail to deliver. Fails are therefore a function of the borrow fee — a noisy, lagged proxy for the exact variable you already bought from Ortex/S3/IBKR. Muravyev/Pearson/Pollet (JFE 2025) then show the option-implied borrow fee subsumes the indicative fee, utilization, AND short interest in joint regressions, placing FTD at the bottom of an already-dominated measurement hierarchy. And the timing is fatal: SEC FTD files publish twice monthly with roughly a 3-week lag, so the freshest observation is ~2 weeks stale and the oldest ~5 weeks, while borrow fee and utilization update intraday. A 2-5 week stale proxy cannot "confirm" a fast-moving constraint state.
referee.who_is_on_other_side:
Four counterparties, each paid in cash, up front, for exactly the risk you want to take.

(1) SHARE LENDERS — agent lenders, prime brokers, and retail fully-paid-lending programs — collect 30-150%+ annualized on these names. They are the structural winners of the entire short-constraint anomaly. The arithmetic is explicit in the literature: Drechsler's CME portfolio goes from 1.31%/mo gross to 0.78%/mo net, so ~40% of the premium is handed to lenders; Muravyev/Pearson/Pollet's more careful and comprehensive measurement (162 anomalies, JF 2025) says essentially 100% of it is. The lender takes the other side rationally because they earn a guaranteed, daily-accrued, collateralized fee with no directional risk, while you take unbounded left-tail exposure.

(2) OPTION MARKET MAKERS who fail rather than borrow (Evans et al. 2009). They monetize the identical constraint at lower cost than you can, because regulation lets them short without borrowing. Their fails are literally the "signal" you are reading. You are trying to trade on the footprint of someone who is already extracting the value more cheaply — and the paper notes the residual profit accrues to the market maker, with larger market makers holding the cost advantage.

(3) MOMENTUM AND RETAIL BUYERS of the squeeze tail. They supply the +615% to +2,168% observations that determine your mean. They are not rational in the classical sense, but they do not need to be — they only need to exist, and the data shows they reliably do.

(4) MARKET MAKERS IN THE MICROCAP ITSELF, earning the 1-3% round-trip spread on every entry and exit you make.

Note the asymmetry: every one of these parties is paid immediately and with certainty, while your payoff is a small median drift that arrives slowly and is contingent on not being bought in.
referee.frictions:
Cost stack for a representative $1.50 chronic-fail short, 14-day hold, per unit of notional.

GROSS EDGE (most favorable trim, upper tail >1.8x removed): +1.02%.

- BORROW FEE: chronic failers are hard-to-borrow by definition. Verified public examples of HTB rates: BYND 152.1%, LMNL 80.4%, HEAR 45.1%. IBKR notes the least liquid shares can exceed 100% annualized. At a mid-range 50%/yr: 50% x 14/365 = 1.92%. At 100%: 3.84%. Rate is NOT locked — it resets daily and can spike overnight.
- COMMISSION: IBKR Pro fixed is $0.005/share, minimum $1, maximum 1% of trade value. On a $1.50 stock that is 0.333% each way = 0.67% round trip. On a $0.50 stock $0.005/share = 1.0%, which hits the cap, giving 1% each way = 2.0% round trip. IBKR also flags additional ECN charges for removing liquidity on stocks under $2.50 — precisely this cohort.
- SPREAD: the $0.01 minimum tick is a hard floor of 0.67% on a $1.50 stock and 1.0% on a $1.00 stock. Realistic quoted microcap spreads are $0.02-0.05, i.e. 1.3-3.3%. Published guidance puts small-cap spreads at 500+ bps in the tail and notes 100 bps means 1% in and 1% out. Use 1.3% round trip as a favorable estimate.
- MARGIN DRAG: FINRA Rule 4210 requires, for a short in a stock under $5, maintenance margin of $2.50/share OR 100% of market value, whichever is GREATER. On a $1.50 stock that is $2.50 against $1.50 of exposure = 167% of notional; on a $1.00 stock, 250%. Capital efficiency is 0.4x-0.6x, so every return figure on notional must be multiplied by ~0.4-0.6 to get return on capital.
- COMPANION DATA: Ortex Basic $39/mo ($348/yr), Advanced $129/mo ($948/yr). S3/Markit institutional feeds are materially more. IBKR provides indicative borrow rate, availability, lender count, historical rates, and a Securities Lending Dashboard with utilization, shares on loan and short interest indicators — FREE to account holders. SEC FTD data is free.
- TAXES: short-sale gains are ALWAYS short-term ordinary income regardless of holding period. At a 35-40% marginal rate, any surviving positive expectancy is cut by more than a third.

TOTAL round-trip cost, favorable assumptions: 1.92% (borrow) + 0.67% (commission) + 1.3% (spread) = 3.9% against a +1.02% gross edge. NET ≈ -2.9% per 14-day cycle on notional, roughly -55%/yr, and worse on capital after the margin multiplier. Even in the physically impossible case of zero spread and zero commission, the borrow fee alone (1.92%) is nearly 2x the gross edge.

OPTIONS ROUTE (the analyst's "only version worth testing"): most sub-$5 microcaps have no listed options at all; those that do quote $0.05-0.50 wide markets on $0.50-1.50 premiums, i.e. 10-50% of premium in round-trip spread, against IV levels of 100-200%+ that already embed the borrow fee. Muravyev/Pearson/Pollet's central result is that option-implied vol mechanically reflects the borrow fee — so the put is priced off the very drift you are trying to buy. Paying 20-30% of premium in spread to harvest a ~1%/2wk drift that the option already prices is not a close call.
referee.capacity:
PER TRADE: The chronic sub-$5 cohort is genuinely microcap. Median fail notional in the chronic $0.50-5 group is $12,962 (25th pct $2,341; 75th pct $62,888). Fail notional is not ADV, but it scales with it, and these names typically trade $50k-$1M/day. Holding to ~5-10% of ADV to keep impact near the 0.3-0.5% level implies $5,000-$25,000 per name. Above that, impact on a name with a $0.01-0.05 spread swamps a 1%-scale edge immediately.

BREADTH: ~215 distinct chronic names priced $0.50-5 exist on any given settlement date (median 201, 10th pct 155, 90th pct 297, over 2,660 dates 2015-2026). Breadth is adequate; size per name is not.

PER YEAR: 200 names x $15k = ~$3M gross short notional at any time. With ~26 two-week cycles that is $75-150M of annual turnover — but the binding constraint is capital, not turnover. FINRA 4210's max($2.50/share, 100% of market value) means $3M of sub-$5 short exposure requires roughly $5-7.5M of dedicated equity. So a fund would tie up $5-7.5M to carry $3M of exposure whose gross edge is ~30%/yr at the most generous measurement and whose borrow cost alone is 30-100%/yr on that notional.

REALISTIC CAPACITY FOR POSITIVE NET EDGE: zero. The expectancy is negative at every plausible size, so capacity is not size-limited — it is sign-limited. There is no trade size at which this makes money. For completeness, if the gross edge were real at the most favorable trim, the strategy would still be capped around $2-3M gross short before impact alone consumed it, which cannot support the $948/yr data cost plus the operational burden for a small fund, and is far below institutional relevance.
referee.decay_evidence:
ALREADY ARBITRAGED, AND THE ARBITRAGEUR IS THE LENDER, NOT A COMPETING TRADER.

(1) The definitive result: Muravyev, Pearson & Pollet, "Anomalies and Their Short-Sale Costs," Journal of Finance 80(6), Dec 2025, pp. 3639-3694. Across a comprehensive sample of 162 anomalies, the average long-short portfolio returns 0.14%/month before short-sale costs and -0.01%/month after borrow fees. Returns come entirely from the short leg. Most damning for THIS strategy specifically: anomalies are not profitable even BEFORE fees once the high-fee observations — 12% of stock-dates — are excluded. The alpha lives exclusively in the high-fee names, and the fee is exactly the size of the alpha. This strategy proposes to concentrate deliberately in that 12%. The paper is a direct, recent, top-journal refutation of the trade's premise, and it postdates and supersedes the more optimistic Drechsler net-of-fee figure.

(2) Muravyev, Pearson & Pollet, "Why Does Options Market Information Predict Stock Returns?", JFE 2025: return predictability from IV spread and skew falls by at least two-thirds when high-fee stocks are excluded, and the option-implied borrow fee subsumes indicative fee, utilization and short interest. The University of Illinois Gies release summarizes it as "borrowing fee is the variable that debunks theory that options predict future stock returns." Every input in this strategy collapses into one already-priced variable.

(3) FULLY COMMERCIALIZED, ZERO INFORMATIONAL MOAT. Ortex sells short interest, utilization, cost-to-borrow and days-to-cover at $39-129/mo, sourced from 700k+ liquidity pools across agent lenders, prime brokers and broker-dealers, with a claimed 97% accuracy against exchange-reported SI, and it ALSO publishes an FTD field in its API. S3 Partners and Markit/IHS sell the institutional versions. IBKR gives indicative rates, availability, lender counts, historical rates and a full Securities Lending Dashboard (utilization, shares on loan, SI) free. SEC FTD data is free and is already re-published by ForcedAlpha, ChartExchange, Stocksera and Fintel. There is nothing here that is not on a retail dashboard for $39/month — which answers the research question directly: the companion data is cheap and retail-accessible, and that is precisely the problem, not the solution.

(4) The stock-lending market prices this in real time. Muravyev/Pearson/Pollet (JF 2022) find the risk premium in lending fees is small and that borrowing-fee risk does not predict fee-adjusted returns — i.e. lenders set fees efficiently against the expected decline, leaving nothing on the table.

(5) General factor decay: measured factor half-lives have compressed from ~60 months for 2005-2010 vintages to ~18 months for 2020-2024 vintages, and crowding accelerated post-2015. A mechanical, fully-published, freely-computable signal is the worst possible profile for surviving this.
referee.net_edge_estimate:
NEGATIVE, AND THE GROSS COMPONENT IS NOT EVEN SIGN-IDENTIFIABLE.

Point estimate on the most favorable defensible reading: gross +1.02% per 14-day cycle; costs 1.92% borrow (at 50%/yr) + 0.67% commission + 1.3% spread = 3.9%; NET ≈ -2.9% per cycle on notional, ≈ -55%/yr, and roughly -1.2% to -1.7% per cycle on capital after the 167-250% FINRA 4210 margin multiplier. Before short-term-ordinary-income tax, which only matters if the sign were positive.

The uncertainty is not symmetric noise around this — the gross input itself is unknowable from the available data, and I want to be explicit about that rather than manufacture a confidence interval. On the horizon-matched panel the mean flips sign purely on where the upper tail is trimmed: -1.02% (trim >1.8x), -0.61% (>3x), -0.34% (>5x), +0.19% (>10x), +0.83% (>25x), with untrimmed mean +7.29% and max +899,900%. Fewer than 0.6% of observations control the sign. Because the FTD file carries unadjusted prior-day closes, genuine squeezes and reverse splits are inseparable in that tail, and short P&L treats them oppositely (a squeeze is a real loss; a reverse split is a non-event). Resolving this requires split-adjusted price data that is NOT in the FTD archive, so the gross expectancy CANNOT be estimated from this dataset — I will not put a number on it and pretend otherwise.

That indeterminacy is itself the finding. Every honest trim leaves a gross edge of at most ~1%/2wk, and the borrow fee alone at a mid-range 50% HTB rate is 1.92%/2wk. The cost floor exceeds the ceiling of the edge. No refinement of the signal changes that ordering, which is why the answer does not depend on resolving the tail.

Independent corroboration that the correct net answer is ~zero-to-negative: Muravyev/Pearson/Pollet (JF 2025) measure -0.01%/month net of borrow fees across 162 anomalies, with the alpha concentrated in exactly the 12% high-fee stock-dates this strategy targets. My bottom-up cost stack and their top-down measurement agree.
referee.barriers:
Beyond the negative expectancy, the operational barriers are individually disqualifying for a small trader.

(1) YOU OFTEN CANNOT BORROW AT ALL. Chronic failers are chronic failers precisely because shares are unavailable — the fails ARE the unavailability. IBKR's SLB screen will frequently show zero shares or zero lenders on exactly the names the screen selects. The signal is anti-correlated with your ability to act on it: the stronger the signal, the less likely the trade exists.

(2) BUY-IN AND RECALL RISK. Hard-to-borrow shorts get recalled without notice, and recalls cluster during squeezes — you are force-covered at the worst possible price, converting the fat right tail from a paper loss into a realized one. This risk is absent from every backtest, including the analyst's.

(3) BORROW RATE IS NOT LOCKED. It resets daily. A position entered at 30% can be at 300% within days, and the 2-week holding period gives the rate ample time to move against you.

(4) FINRA RULE 4210. Shorting a sub-$5 stock requires maintenance margin of $2.50/share or 100% of market value, whichever is greater — 167% of notional on a $1.50 stock, 250% on a $1.00 stock. Roughly half to two-fifths of your capital is productive.

(5) MANY RETAIL BROKERS SIMPLY PROHIBIT shorting stocks under $5, and some prohibit odd lots. The cohort where the entire (already-refuted) signal lives may be off-limits by broker policy.

(6) DATA STALENESS. SEC FTD publishes twice monthly with roughly a 3-week lag; observations are 2-5 weeks old on arrival. Any strategy needing FTD to "confirm" a live borrow-fee state is confirming with information older than the state itself.

(7) SUB-$2.50 ECN FEES. IBKR explicitly flags extra ECN charges for removing liquidity on stocks under $2.50, an additional cost concentrated in this exact cohort.

(8) THE OPTIONS ESCAPE HATCH IS CLOSED. Most of these names have no listed options; where they exist, spreads run 10-50% of premium and IV already embeds the borrow fee by the mechanism Muravyev/Pearson/Pollet document.

(9) OPERATIONAL LOAD. ~200 positions of $5-25k each, rebalanced fortnightly, in the most fraud-prone, promotion-prone, halt-prone corner of the US market — for a negative expected return.
referee.confidence:
HIGH — unusually so, because this rests on a reproduced computational finding rather than only on judgment.

What makes it high:

referee.strategy: Create-to-Lend Borrow-Fee Harvest on XRT-type "hard-to-borrow" ETFs: buy and hold a persistently high-short-interest sector ETF, enroll the shares in a retail fully-paid lending program (IBKR SYEP / Fidelity FPL / Schwab SLFP), hedge the market exposure, and harvest the cost-to-borrow as net carry.
referee.edge_case:
The strongest honest case is a real, documented market anomaly — but one the retail version cannot reach. Andrews, Henderson and Reed ("ETF Lending Premia and the Limits of Create-to-Lend Arbitrage," SSRN 4667997) document that the median ETF lending fee is 300bp versus 37.5bp for stocks — 8x — and that fewer than 18% of ETFs lend below 100bp versus roughly 80% of stocks. They size ETF abnormal loan fees at ~$4.4bn in 2024. They also show create-to-lend "caps but does not eliminate" the premium, i.e. there is genuine residual economic rent in ETF lending that arbitrage does not fully compete away. So the underlying phenomenon is real and academically confirmed, not folklore.

The mechanics of the retail leg are also real and verifiable: IBKR SYEP pays 50% of the market rate with 100% collateral in US Treasuries or cash held in a segregated pledge account; Fidelity FPL pays a 60/40 split in the lender's favor plus a 26.98% credit adjustment on the qualified portion of cash-in-lieu distributions; Schwab SLFP is 50/50. These are genuine, low-effort income streams on shares you already intend to own, and on a genuinely special name the income can matter.

The most defensible residual version of this idea is the unhedged one: if you already want long retail-sector exposure for independent reasons, enrolling in fully-paid lending is a free-option overlay worth roughly 25-55bp/yr on XRT. That is a real, if tiny, enhancement — but it is an expense-ratio offset, not a strategy, and it carries no market-neutral carry claim whatsoever.
referee.against_case:
The case against is overwhelming and operates at three independent levels, any one of which is fatal.

FIRST — THE PREMISE IS FACTUALLY FALSE. XRT is not hard to borrow. As of 2026-08-12 the IBKR borrow fee on XRT was 1.07% with 500,000 shares available (ChartExchange, IBKR feed). That is essentially general collateral; S3 Partners puts typical GC at ~30bp, so XRT is a rounding error above GC and nowhere near "special." The >100% short interest is an ETF artifact, not evidence of scarcity: MarketBeat shows 20,468,454 shares short as of 2026-07-31 against roughly 2-5.5M shares outstanding (568.57% of float), but ETF shares are created on demand, the denominator is elastic, and the same shares can be re-lent along a chain. Even at the absolute peak of the January-March 2021 meme-stock mania, S3's Ihor Dusaniwsky publicly noted XRT borrowed at 2.32% — while GME itself was 1.70%. XRT has never been meaningfully special.

Worse, the causality runs backwards from the thesis. The Andrews/Henderson/Reed paper finds that a single "short favorite" typically intermediates most shorting at relatively low fees, while close substitutes with unfavorable ownership structures carry the high abnormal fees. XRT is the short favorite. Its short interest is enormous precisely BECAUSE it is cheap and liquid to borrow. High short interest and high borrow fee are substitutes in the ETF loan market, not complements. Screening on short interest to find lending income systematically selects the cheapest names to lend.

SECOND — THE FEE IS FULLY PRICED INTO THE HEDGE. I tested this directly against live CBOE delayed quotes (2026-08-13, XRT spot 88.99, bid/ask 88.99/89.00, IV30 21.78%). Backing the implied borrow out of put-call parity across the liquid strikes, using rf=3.81% and the actual $0.1865 quarterly dividend schedule: Sep-18-26 K=85 implies 0.79%, Dec-18-26 K=85 implies 1.11%, Jan-15-27 K=90 implies 1.43%, Jan-15-27 K=85 implies 1.57%. Center of mass ~1.1-1.4% against a quoted cash borrow of 1.07%. The options market charges the full borrow fee, accurately, with no exploitable gap. This is exactly what the literature predicts — Atmaz ("Option Prices and Costly Short-Selling") and the Illinois/Gies work showing the borrow fee acts as a "shadow dividend" in option pricing.

THIRD — THE ALGEBRA IS UNCONDITIONALLY DOMINATED. A conversion-hedged holder earns rf − borrow, because the option leg charges the full fee. Add back lending income of split × borrow × utilization. Total = rf − borrow × (1 − split × util). For ANY borrow > 0 and ANY split < 100%, this is STRICTLY BELOW the risk-free rate. At IBKR's 50% split and 100% utilization: 3.27% vs 3.81% T-bills, −54bp before a single commission. At Fidelity's 60%: 3.38%, −43bp. At 50% utilization: 3.01%, −80bp. There is no borrow fee that rescues it — a HIGHER fee makes the trade WORSE, because you pay 100% of it in the hedge and recover only 50-60%. The strategy is not marginal; it is structurally, mathematically upside-down.
referee.who_is_on_other_side:
Three well-capitalized parties, each rationally and structurally advantaged over the retail lender.

AUTHORIZED PARTICIPANTS RUNNING THE REAL CREATE-TO-LEND TRADE. State Street's own ETF education material lists create-to-lend as a standard AP motive, noting that those "with the tactical flexibility to create to lend when borrow rates increase" benefit. The AP assembles the underlying basket, delivers it for a 50,000-share creation unit, lends the resulting ETF shares, and hedges the residual exposure. Crucially the AP captures 100% of the lending fee, not 50%, finances at institutional repo rather than paying an option-implied borrow, and can redeem the shares the moment the fee compresses. Their economics are the retail trade's economics plus the entire 50% haircut plus the entire hedge cost. They rationally take the other side because they are earning the spread between the ETF lending fee and the composite borrow cost of the underlying basket — the very spread that caps the fee at the ~1% level I measured.

OPTIONS MARKET MAKERS. They will happily sell you the conversion at a mid-market implied borrow of ~1.1-1.4% and pocket the bid-ask. They are indifferent to your thesis; they have simply priced the carry correctly and charge 34-95 cents of width on an $89 underlying for the privilege of getting it wrong in their favor.

THE BROKER ITSELF. IBKR, Fidelity and Schwab are the true beneficiaries. They keep 40-50% of the fee for an operationally trivial intermediation, and they already have a cheaper supply: shares in margin accounts, rehypothecable under Reg T at no cost to the broker at all. Fully-paid retail shares are drawn on only after that free inventory is exhausted — which for a 1.07% name with 500,000 shares openly available at IBKR plainly has not happened. This is why realized utilization on a GC-ish name is the quiet killer: you are the marginal, last-in-line supplier of a commodity the broker can already source for free.
referee.frictions:
Built against live quotes, not estimates. Underlying: XRT $88.78-88.99, AUM $484.73M, expense ratio 0.35%, ADV 3,714,896 shares, dividend $0.1865/qtr (0.76% yield), IV30 21.78%.

XRT STOCK SPREAD: $0.01 on $89.00 = 1.1bp. Genuinely negligible; this is the one cheap leg, and etf.com-type sources put XRT spreads around 0.02% vs a 0.13% ETF average.

OPTION SPREADS — THE DOMINANT COST. This is where the trade dies. Live ATM widths: Sep-18-26 K=90 call 1.86/2.20 (34c) and put 2.78/3.15 (37c); Sep-18-26 K=85 call 4.80/5.75 (95c); Jan-15-27 K=85 call 7.90/8.65 (75c), put 3.70/3.90 (20c); Jan-15-27 K=90 call 5.05/5.95 (90c), put 5.60/6.35 (75c). Combined round-trip crossing cost on a conversion is 55c-165c on an $89 underlying = 62-185bp of notional. Open interest away from a handful of strikes is in the single digits and most strikes printed ZERO volume, so the quoted width is optimistic, not conservative.

ACTUAL EXECUTED CONVERSION P&L (buy stock at ask, buy put at ask, sell call at bid, dividends credited, IBKR commissions of $0.005/share plus $0.65/contract each way = ~3.6c per 100 shares round trip):
- Sep-18-26 K=90: outlay 90.290, receive 90.000 → −3.66%/yr
- Sep-18-26 K=85: outlay 85.300, receive 85.000 → −3.99%/yr
- Dec-18-26 K=85: outlay 85.050, receive 85.186 → +0.34%/yr
- Jan-15-27 K=85: outlay 85.000, receive 85.373 → +0.93%/yr (best case found)
- Jan-15-27 K=90: outlay 90.300, receive 90.373 → +0.10%/yr
Mid-to-mid these look like +0.8% to +3.2%/yr; executable they collapse to −4.0% to +0.9%/yr. The entire apparent edge lives inside the bid-ask spread.

BORROW FEE RECEIVED: 1.07% gross × 50% (IBKR/Schwab) or 60% (Fidelity) = 53-64bp at 100% utilization; realistically 13-32bp at the 25-50% utilization plausible for a near-GC name competing with free rehypothecated margin inventory.

TAX DRAG: dividends arrive as payment-in-lieu, taxed as ordinary income rather than qualified. On XRT's $0.746/yr dividend a 17-20pp rate differential costs ~13-15bp/yr — which alone consumes 25-30% of the gross lending income. Fidelity's 26.98% credit adjustment partially offsets this; IBKR and Schwab offer no such adjustment.

EXPENSE RATIO: 0.35%/yr. Washes out under an XRT-options hedge (embedded in both legs) but is a full 35bp drag under any cross-hedge.

TOTAL STACK vs the 3.81% 3-month T-bill: best realistic case ~0.74-0.84%/yr, worst case negative. Shortfall of roughly 300-350bp/yr.
referee.capacity:
Capacity analysis is almost beside the point — the trade is negative-expectancy at $1, so its "capacity" is zero in any economically meaningful sense — but the scale numbers independently confirm it is not worth building infrastructure for.

The entire lendable universe is trivially small. XRT's total fund value is $182-485M depending on source (sources conflict badly: stockanalysis reports 2.05M shares outstanding alongside $484.73M AUM, which is internally inconsistent at an $88.78 price; MarketBeat reports 3.6M shares; the AUM figure implies ~5.46M). Across that entire range, the GROSS lending fee pool generated by every single share of XRT in existence at 1.07% is only $1.95M-$5.19M per year — and that is before the 40-50% broker haircut, and it is split among every holder on earth, dominated by index funds and institutional agent-lending programs already enrolled.

Per-trade liquidity is genuinely fine: ADV of 3.71M shares is ~$330M/day, so $5-25M could be assembled in the ETF leg without meaningful impact. The binding constraint is the option leg, where most strikes showed zero daily volume and single-digit open interest — a $25M conversion would need ~2,800 contracts per leg against strikes routinely showing OI under 100. That is not executable at quoted width; you would move the implied borrow against yourself immediately.

Realistic per-trade capacity for a small fund is therefore ~$1-5M, constrained by option depth, and annual capacity is not additive in any useful way since the position simply sits.

The opportunity cost at those sizes: $1M deployed earns ~$5,350/yr in lending income versus $38,100 in T-bills — forgoing $32,750. $5M forgoes $163,750/yr. $25M forgoes $818,750/yr. You are paying roughly 3% per year for the privilege of running a complex, operationally demanding, counterparty-exposed position.
referee.decay_evidence:
This is not a decaying edge; it is a fully commercialized institutional business that retail is being sold the scraps of.

ALREADY INDUSTRIALIZED AT THE FUND LEVEL. State Street runs securities lending on XRT's own underlying holdings and markets it explicitly ("Unlock the potential in your portfolio with securities lending," "Unlocking the securities lending potential of SPY"). Morningstar covers securities lending as a mainstream expense-ratio-offset mechanism. Every large agent lender — State Street, BlackRock, Goldman, Northern Trust — has been harvesting this for decades at 100% of the fee with institutional balance sheets.

THE RETAIL PROGRAMS *ARE* THE COMMERCIALIZED PRODUCT. IBKR SYEP, Fidelity FPL, Schwab SLFP and M1's FPSL exist precisely to aggregate retail supply into this institutional market. The 40-50% haircut IS the vendor's take. There is no undiscovered edge here to be arbitraged away — the arbitrage has been packaged, priced, and sold, and the retail participant is the supplier of raw material, not the beneficiary.

CREATE-TO-LEND HAS ALREADY COMPETED THE FEE DOWN ON EXACTLY THIS NAME. The Andrews/Henderson/Reed finding is that create-to-lend caps the premium, and the cap binds hardest on liquid, heavily-created, heavily-shorted names with many APs — which is the exact description of XRT. My measured 1.07% versus a ~30bp GC baseline and a median ETF fee of 300bp shows XRT sitting near the bottom of the ETF fee distribution. The competition has already happened and XRT lost. Where the abnormal fees persist is in illiquid substitute ETFs with concentrated sole-voting ownership ("local lending oligopolies") — names a small trader cannot accumulate in size, cannot hedge (no liquid options), and cannot exit.

THE OPTIONS MARKET SHOWS ZERO RESIDUAL. Live parity-implied borrow of 0.79-1.57% straddles the quoted 1.07% cash fee. If any harvestable gap existed between what lenders receive and what the hedge costs, it would show up as a systematic wedge here. It does not.

CONSISTENT WITH THE ANALYST'S PRIOR FTD RESULT. This is the same failure mode as naive FTD spike signals: a dramatic, widely-publicized surface statistic (568% short interest) that is a mechanical artifact of ETF creation/redemption rather than evidence of scarcity or stress. The FTD work found only chronic-persistence-plus-low-price survived; here, not even a conditional version survives, because the conditioning variable (borrow fee) is directly observable and directly priced by a liquid options market. There is no hidden state left to exploit.
referee.net_edge_estimate:
Net-of-cost expectancy is NEGATIVE relative to the risk-free rate, with unusually high confidence because the result is algebraic rather than statistical.

CENTRAL ESTIMATE (options-hedged, the only genuinely market-neutral version): +0.3% to +0.9%/yr total return, against a 3.81% 3-month T-bill. Net expectancy of roughly −290 to −350bp/yr. Decomposition at the best executable structure found (Jan-15-27 K=85 conversion): +0.93%/yr executed conversion carry, plus 13-64bp lending income depending on split and utilization, minus 13-15bp payment-in-lieu tax drag = 0.93% to 1.44%/yr gross, and that best case relies on the single tightest strike in the entire chain. Every shorter-dated structure I priced came out between −3.66% and +0.34%/yr. Probability-weighted across realistic execution, roughly 0.5%/yr.

CROSS-HEDGED VARIANT (short XLY/RTH instead of options): 3.81% collateral + 0.54% lending − 0.35% expense ratio − ~0.30% hedge borrow = 3.69%/yr, i.e. −12bp versus T-bills — while assuming full XRT-vs-XLY basis risk. XRT is equal-weighted and includes small-cap retail; XLY is cap-weighted and dominated by Amazon and Tesla. Realistic tracking error is high single to low double digits annualized. You would be accepting perhaps 8-12% of annualized basis volatility to earn approximately zero. Risk-adjusted this is worse than the options version, not better.

UNHEDGED VARIANT: you collect 13-64bp/yr while carrying 21.78% implied volatility of directional retail-sector exposure. Carry-to-vol of roughly 0.02. This is not a carry trade; it is a directional bet with a rounding error attached.

THE UNCERTAINTY IS SMALL AND ONE-SIDED, WHICH IS THE KEY POINT. The genuinely unknown inputs are realized SYEP utilization (I could not verify XRT-specific fill rates — IBKR's pages return 403 and no broker publishes per-symbol utilization) and forward borrow-fee path. But both uncertainties push the wrong way: lower utilization lowers income, and a HIGHER borrow fee makes the hedged trade strictly worse, since you pay 100% of the fee in the option leg and recover only 50-60%. The dominance result — rf − borrow × (1 − split × util) < rf for all borrow > 0 and all split < 1 — holds for every parameter value in the admissible range. I cannot construct a parameterization where this trade beats Treasury bills.

WHAT I COULD NOT VERIFY: exact realized SYEP utilization on XRT; IBKR's precise wholesale "market rate" versus the 1.07% retail short charge (the wholesale rate is typically LOWER, which would further reduce the 53bp figure); and the full historical XRT borrow-fee time series behind ChartExchange's and iBorrowDesk's paywalls. I have flagged rather than estimated these. None would change the sign.
referee.barriers:
THE LITERAL "CREATE-TO-LEND" LEG IS STRUCTURALLY UNAVAILABLE. The profitable version of this trade requires being an Authorized Participant. SPDR creation units are 50,000 shares — ~$4.45M per unit at $89 — and creation requires being a DTC Participant with an executed Authorized Participant Agreement with the fund's distributor. Only a few dozen broker-dealers globally qualify. A small trader cannot create shares, cannot redeem them when the fee compresses, and therefore cannot run the strategy the name describes. They can only buy shares in the secondary market and lend them at a 40-50% haircut, which is a strictly worse instrument.

THE MANDATORY HAIRCUT. Every retail venue takes 40-50%: IBKR 50%, Schwab 50%, Fidelity 60/40 in the lender's favor. Since the hedge charges 100% of the fee, this haircut alone guarantees a loss on the hedged trade. There is no retail venue offering a split above 100%, and there cannot be.

NO CONTROL OVER UTILIZATION. You cannot choose when your shares are lent. The broker lends its free rehypothecated margin inventory first (Reg T permits use of customer margin securities at no cost), and taps fully-paid retail supply only when that is exhausted. For XRT — 1.07% fee, 500,000 shares openly available at IBKR — that condition is not met. You are last in the queue for a commodity in surplus.

ENROLLMENT AND LOCK-IN GATES. IBKR requires a margin account or a cash account with liquid net worth above $25,000, and imposes a 90-day wait before re-enrolling if you leave. Schwab requires $100,000 in household assets AND is invitation-only, subject to Schwab's approval — you may simply not be allowed in. ERISA accounts (401(k)s) are excluded entirely.

COUNTERPARTY AND REHYPOTHECATION RISK — THE ASYMMETRY THAT MATTERS. Securities on loan are NOT covered by SIPC. You are unsecured against your own broker, protected only by collateral: IBKR posts 100% in US Treasuries or cash in a segregated pledge account; Fidelity posts a minimum of 100% USD collateral with a third-party custodian. Note that 100% collateral against a position marked daily still leaves gap risk in a fast market, and the collateral is marked to yesterday's close. You are accepting a small probability of a large loss in exchange for 53bp — a profoundly unattractive risk shape, and one that is worst precisely in the stressed markets where a retail sector ETF would gap.

LOSS OF VOTING RIGHTS AND QUALIFIED DIVIDEND TREATMENT while on loan, with only Fidelity offering partial (26.98%) compensation.

EARLY ASSIGNMENT ON THE SHORT CALL. American-style XRT options mean the short call in a conversion can be assigned around ex-dividend, stripping the stock, killing the lending income, and leaving a naked long put. This is not theoretical — it is the standard outcome for a deep-ITM short call before a dividend.

OPERATIONAL COMPLEXITY WILDLY DISPROPORTIONATE TO REWARD. Managing a rolling conversion, monitoring assignment risk, tracking lending accruals and cash-in-lieu tax lots, all to underperform a T-bill ladder by ~3%/yr.
referee.confidence:
HIGH — and higher than I am normally willing to be on a rejection, for three specific reasons.

1. THE CORE RESULT IS ALGEBRAIC, NOT STATISTICAL. It requires no backtest, no sample period, and no distributional assumption. An options-hedged lender earns rf − borrow × (1 − split × util). For any positive borrow fee and any split below 100%, that is strictly less than rf. There is no parameter choice — no borrow fee, no utilization rate, no volatility regime — that flips the sign. This is not "the edge is probably too small"; it is "the edge has the wrong sign by construction." I stress-tested it at 50% and 60% splits and at 25%, 50% and 100% utilization; all nine combinations lose to T-bills before costs.

2. THE FACTUAL PREMISE IS DIRECTLY FALSIFIED BY OBSERVED DATA, NOT INFERENCE. The strategy is predicated on XRT being persistently hard to borrow with a high sustained fee. The measured fee is 1.07% with 500,000 shares freely available (ChartExchange/IBKR, 2026-08-12). Even at the peak of the 2021 meme-stock episode, S3's Ihor Dusaniwsky publicly noted XRT at 2.32% — cheaper to short than GME at 1.70%. The premise is not merely optimistic; it is inverted, and the academic literature explains why: XRT is the "short favorite" that intermediates most shorting AT LOW FEES, which is exactly why its short interest is 568% of float.

3. I VERIFIED THE HEDGE-PRICING CLAIM EMPIRICALLY RATHER THAN ASSUMING IT. Rather than asserting that options price the borrow, I pulled live CBOE quotes and inverted put-call parity across every liquid strike with a proper dividend schedule. Implied borrow came out at 0.79%, 1.11%, 1.43% and 1.57% against a 1.07% quoted cash fee. The options market has it right to within the bid-ask. That closes the only loophole through which this trade could have worked.

CALIBRATION AND WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY MIND. My confidence is in the VERDICT, not in every input. Three numbers I could not verify and have flagged rather than fabricated: XRT-specific realized SYEP utilization (no broker publishes it; IBKR's own pages returned HTTP 403 to every fetch attempt, so all IBKR program terms here come from secondary sources and IBKR's own guides subdomain rather than the primary pricing page); IBKR's wholesale lending rate versus the 1.07% retail short charge; and the paywalled long-run XRT fee history. Critically, all three uncertainties push the conclusion in the SAME direction — the wholesale rate is typically below the retail short charge, and lower utilization means less income — so resolving them can only make the trade worse.

I would revisit only on a genuinely different setup: a lender split above 100% (does not exist), an ETF where option-implied borrow sits materially BELOW the achievable lending rate (I found the opposite), or AP status enabling real create-to-lend with full fee capture and redemption optionality. None is available to a small trader. This same failure mode — a dramatic surface statistic (568% short interest) that is a mechanical artifact rather than evidence of scarcity — is precisely the pattern the analyst's FTD work already identified. Recommend declining without further work.

referee.strategy: Illiquid-Underlying ETF NAV-Discount Convergence — buying HY/muni/bank-loan/EM bond ETFs when they trade at a wide, persistent discount to NAV during market stress, on the thesis that APs will eventually arbitrage the gap closed (March 2020 as case study).
referee.edge_case:
The discounts are real, large, and documented. Verified magnitudes from March 2020: LQD traded at a 5.08% discount on 3/19/2020; AGG and BND at 4.43% and 6.17% on 3/16/2020; IG corporate bond ETFs averaged roughly a 3.4% discount in mid-March with some products beyond 8%. BIS (Quarterly Review, March 2021, "The anatomy of bond ETF arbitrage") reports bond ETF tracking error exceeded 200bp for some funds in March-April 2020 versus a 0.7bp historical sector average — a ~300x dislocation. The mechanism that should produce convergence is genuine and mechanical: APs can redeem in kind and sell the bonds, which is a far harder constraint to evade than in closed-end funds.

The economic case is that during a dash-for-cash, forced sellers pay a large premium for immediacy while the natural buyers (AP/dealer balance sheets) are simultaneously constrained. Pan & Zeng ("ETF Arbitrage under Liquidity Mismatch") document precisely this: most APs are also bond dealers using one balance sheet for both roles, and large bond flow shocks to AP balance sheets limit ETF arbitrage, "leading to persistent relative mispricings." That is a textbook limits-to-arbitrage setup, and someone with unconstrained capital genuinely does get paid for supplying liquidity there.

And the discounts did resolve: BIS notes steep discounts "transformed into large premiums" within days. Prices did rebound hard — LQD +16.8% in 5 days from 3/19, EMB +14.2% from 3/18, MUB +13.3% from 3/19 (my computation, Yahoo daily closes).

That is the strongest form of the case. It does not survive contact with the actual timing evidence below.
referee.against_case:
Three independent kills.

1) THE DISCOUNT IS A CORRECT PRICE, NOT A MISPRICING. Bond ETF NAV is struck once daily off vendor matrix marks (ICE/IHS Markit/BVAL) built from surveys and models, not executable bids. BlackRock's own SEC-FIAC deck (July 2020) shows the standard deviation of dealer quotes versus actual trade prices exploding in March 2020 — the NAV inputs themselves were unreliable. The decisive logic, which I found stated plainly in the practitioner literature: if NAV prices were actionable and market makers could sell those bonds meaningfully above the ETF price, the dislocation would have normalized immediately. It did not. BIS confirms the gap "was not arbitraged away" by APs. APs had both the ability and the incentive and declined — revealed preference that the NAV was fiction. Notably, >92% of LQD's underlying bonds DID trade on 3/19/2020 and 74% had an observable print within ~2 hours of the close, so this was not mainly a staleness problem: the marks were simply above where bonds cleared. You are not buying a dollar for 95 cents; you are buying a dollar for a dollar and being told by an accountant it is worth 1.05.

2) SIGNAL IS SWAMPED BY NOISE BY AN ORDER OF MAGNITUDE. My computation from Yahoo daily closes: March 2020 annualized realized vol was LQD 58%, HYG 50%, BKLN 56%, EMB 66%, MUB 44% (versus 1-4% in calm February). LQD's DAILY standard deviation was 3.65%. The entire peak discount was 5.08%. One day of noise is ~72% of the whole signal. Over a 5-day convergence window the noise is ~8.2% against a 5% best-case signal. And the crisis-average discount was far smaller than the headline: BlackRock's own data gives average ABSOLUTE premium/discount for March-April 2020 of just LQD 1.39%, HYG 1.06%, TLT 0.86% (versus 0.13-0.21% in Jan-Feb). So the typical trade is a ~1% signal against 50-60% annualized vol.

3) THE ACTUAL FORWARD RETURNS ARE NEGATIVE. This is the FTD result all over again. I took the entry dates a trader could actually identify ex ante as "wide discount" — 3/11, 3/12, 3/16, 3/17/2020, when the press was already reporting 3-6% discounts — across LQD, HYG, BKLN, EMB, MUB (n=20). Mean 5-day return: -7.88%. Median: -8.91%. Percent negative: 95%. Mean worst drawdown within 10 days: -11.70%. Buying the discount on the dates the discount was visibly wide lost money 19 times out of 20. Only 3/18 and 3/19 — the exact bottom, identifiable only in hindsight — were profitable, and that P&L was created on 3/23 when the Fed announced the SMCCF. HYG then jumped +6.5% in a single day on 4/9/2020 when the Fed extended the facility to high-yield ETFs. This strategy's entire historical track record is a bet on the timing of a central bank announcement, wearing an arbitrage costume.

Exactly parallel to the FTD finding: the naive spike signal has no predictive power because the signal is generated by the same stress that keeps causing losses. But note the disanalogy that makes ETFs worse — the FTD work found a surviving "chronic persistence" pattern. In ETFs the create/redeem mechanism specifically prevents chronic persistence, so the analogous surviving signal does not exist here. Closed-end funds, which lack create/redeem, do sustain persistent structural discounts — but that is a different strategy than the one proposed.
referee.who_is_on_other_side:
The seller into the discount is a rational, informed, liquidity-motivated seller — not a patsy. Bond mutual funds meeting redemptions, risk-parity and vol-target programs mechanically deleveraging, insurers and corporates raising cash. For them the ETF at a 4% discount was the CHEAPEST available exit, not an expensive one: over February-March 2020 the bid-ask on individual IG bonds widened from ~25bp to over 100bp while LQD's own bid-ask stayed below 2bp. Selling the ETF at a discount to a stale mark was strictly better than selling the actual bonds, where the achievable bid was lower still. They are trading a mark they know is not real for cash they know is real. That is rational, and it means the "discount" is largely the difference between an accounting mark and a clearing price.

The buyer is a market maker or AP demanding compensation for warehousing credit and gap risk at the exact moment its own balance sheet, VaR limits and repo funding are most constrained.
