RKT IV 55-58% vs RV30 53.0% / RV90 62.1% — roughly fair. OMF IV 25-31% vs RV26.2% — fair. So in the one name where the thesis is most attractive (UWMC), you are also paying the largest vol premium.

BID-ASK / SLIPPAGE ON THE EQUITY. Mean daily high-low range over the last 60 sessions: UWMC 5.98%, RKT 5.18%, CACC 3.49%, PFSI 2.94%, OMF 2.50%. Because 97% of these filings are post-close, you are forced to trade the next open — the single worst liquidity and widest-spread moment of the session — into an auction that has already absorbed the news. Realistic all-in slippage at the open: 25-75bp for PFSI/OMF/CACC, 75-150bp for UWMC/RKT.

BORROW. I could NOT verify live borrow rates for these specific tickers — chartexchange returned 404 and I did not retrieve a current Fintel quote. I will not invent a number. Structurally: RKT, PFSI, CACC and OMF are large, liquid, index-member names that should sit at or near general collateral, which published sources put at roughly 5-50bp annualized for easy-to-borrow stock. UWMC is the exception and genuinely risky: SFS Corp owns ~83% (down from ~90% at end-2024), so the true float is a fraction of shares outstanding, and reported short interest has run from ~4.6% of shares outstanding to ~11.7% of float. A low-float, heavily-shorted, sub-$2 stock that just took a sponsor rescue is exactly the profile that produces recall risk and squeeze risk. Critically, borrow cost is NOT what kills this trade — see net_edge_estimate: raising borrow from 0.5% to 10% moves the short P&L only from -23.2% to -24.7%. The trade is already dead before financing.

COMMISSIONS. Options ~$0.50-0.65/contract retail; equity near zero. Immaterial relative to a 20-120% option spread. Not the binding constraint.

DATA. The feed is commoditized: StockTitan gives instant 8-K alerts on a Gold tier with free users at 1-minute delay; commercial SEC APIs run $99-2,000/month. You cannot buy a latency advantage that matters because, again, 0 of 62 filings arrived during market hours.

TAXES. Every trade is short-term: 2-8 week options and shorts are 100% short-term capital gain, taxed at ordinary income rates (up to 37% federal plus state). There is no long-term treatment available and no way to defer. This turns a marginal gross edge into a negative net edge, and here the gross edge is already negative.
referee.capacity:
Capacity is the wrong question here — the expectancy is negative, so optimal size is zero. But for completeness, and because it independently rules out a small fund:

PER-TRADE, OPTIONS (the specified expression):
  UWMC: total open interest at the tradeable ATM strike is 1,965 contracts at a $0.10 mid = ~$19,650 of premium in the ENTIRE open interest. Realistic entry without moving the quote: 100-300 contracts = $1,000-3,000 of premium. This is not investable at any professional size; it is a rounding error.
  PFSI: the 10% OTM strike had OI of 3 contracts and no bid. Capacity ~$0.
  CACC: no tradeable near-dated chain. Capacity $0.
  RKT: the only real chain. At K=13 the OI is 1,205 with 1,139 daily volume at a $0.23 mid = roughly $28K of premium turnover per day. Realistic entry $10,000-50,000 of premium per trade.
  UNIVERSE-WIDE OPTIONS CAPACITY: on the order of $25,000-75,000 of premium per event, concentrated almost entirely in RKT.

PER-TRADE, EQUITY SHORT (5% of median daily dollar volume, last 60 sessions):
  RKT $19.10M/day (median $vol $382.0M) — genuinely liquid
  CACC $4.14M/day ($82.9M)
  OMF $2.86M/day ($57.2M)
  UWMC $2.39M/day ($47.8M) — but low float and squeeze-prone
  PFSI $2.25M/day ($45.1M)
  Equity capacity is real, roughly $2-19M per name per day. This is the one dimension that is not binding.

PER YEAR: this is the fatal constraint. Genuine capacity-cut events run ~1.6/year at loanDepot, the single most prolific filer in the sector. Across the whole tradeable universe — and remembering COOP is delisted and OMF structurally cannot generate the signal — you get roughly 3-6 qualifying events per year, and most land in names with no options chain.

So: 3-6 trades/year x $25-75K option premium = $75,000-450,000 of annual premium deployment, with essentially all of it forced into RKT. Even if the edge were real and large — say a heroic +30% net on premium, which the data emphatically does not support — that is $22K-135K of gross annual P&L before taxes. That does not pay for one analyst, let alone a fund. Via equity short you could deploy $10-50M per event, but you would be deploying it into a mean +23% adverse move.

The strategy is capacity-constrained into irrelevance for a fund and cost-constrained into irrelevance for a small trader, before the sign problem is even considered.
referee.decay_evidence:
The honest finding is that this edge did not decay — there is no evidence it ever existed in the tradeable direction. But the surrounding infrastructure is fully commercialized, which forecloses any latency-based version:

ALREADY COMMODITIZED — REAL-TIME FILING ACCESS:
- EDGAR full-text search indexes filings in <60 seconds, free, for everyone.
- StockTitan runs a live SEC filing feed with instant alerts on its Gold tier, 30-second delay for Silver, 1-minute for free users, 2-minute for guests — and layers "Rhea-AI" automated sentiment analysis and predictive impact assessment on top. An automated bearish-filing classifier for retail is already a shipped product.
- Commercial SEC APIs (sec-api.io, tldrfiling, PageCrawl, Apify EDGAR monitors) run $99-2,000/month with sub-second claimed latency.
- Bloomberg (~$25K/yr) and FactSet (~$12K/yr) push real-time filing alerts to every institutional desk in the sector.
There is no proprietary access to buy. Whatever you can see, several thousand better-capitalized desks see simultaneously — and, since 97% of filings are post-close, everyone has all night regardless.

ALREADY COMMERCIALIZED — CREDIT-AGREEMENT/COVENANT EXTRACTION: This exact analytical task is a mature software category. Covenant-monitoring specialists (Lumonic), credit portfolio platforms with covenant modules (Allvue, Oxane Partners, CardoAI, Moody's Lending Suite), document-AI extraction (Kira, Luminance, Harvey, V7 Go, TextMine), and data-spreading vendors (Daloopa, Canoe, Accelex) all productize parsing amendments and extracting facility terms. V7 Go explicitly markets processing of "revolving credit agreements ... with multiple agreements, amendments, and exhibits." If there were alpha in reading warehouse amendments faster, the tooling to harvest it has been sold off the shelf for years.

THE INFORMATION LEADS THE FILING, NOT THE REVERSE: The trade press covered these events contemporaneously and often ahead of the filings — HousingWire ("Homepoint shrinks its lending capacity," "loanDepot starts 2023 with changes to its warehouse credit line agreements"), National Mortgage News ("LoanDepot has cut its funding capacity by $1 billion," "LoanDepot alters another financing agreement"), NMP ("loanDepot Does It Again: Cuts Funding Capacity By $500M For 3rd Time"), Asset Securitization Report. A dedicated specialist press already runs this beat in real time and publishes for free.

STRUCTURAL DECAY OF THE UNIVERSE ITSELF: The opportunity set is shrinking mechanically. COOP was acquired by RKT and delisted 10/1/2025 ($14.2B). Home Point sold its wholesale channel and exited. First Guaranty and Sprout are gone. Consolidation has removed roughly half the names that would generate these events, and the survivors are larger, better-capitalized, and less warehouse-fragile.

ACADEMIC CONTEXT: The Notre Dame study "Who Pays Attention to SEC Form 8-K?" examines exactly this — professional attention to 8-K disclosures measured via RavenPack/Dow Jones and Bloomberg terminal coverage. I did not fetch the full paper, so I am not attributing a specific result to it, but the literature on 8-K attention is well-developed and the routine-disclosure categories are the best-covered part of it.

Note also the analyst's prior finding transfers directly: naive FTD spike signals had no predictive power, and only chronic-persistence-plus-low-price survived. The identical structure applies here. A naive "amendment filed" trigger has no power. The only version with any hope would be a chronic one — sustained multi-quarter aggregate capacity contraction combined with a collapsed share price — and that variable comes from the 10-Q liquidity table with a 40-90 day lag, is public and modeled by every sell-side analyst, and is precisely the pattern already reflected in a stock that has fallen 52-87%.
referee.net_edge_estimate:
Negative, and robustly so. I measured it rather than assuming it.

BACKTEST OF THE SPECIFIED PUT EXPRESSION. Applied to the 8 genuine capacity-cut events at loanDepot — the most stressed, most prolific nonbank filer, i.e. the best case available. Trade: buy 60-day 10%-OTM put at signal, exit 40 trading days later, paying half the quoted spread each way. Base case IV 65%, spread 35% of mid (both generous — UWMC's actual spread is 100-120% and its actual IV is 85-89%):

  Premium paid: 6.47% of spot (vs 5.51% theoretical mid — the spread alone costs 17% of the position before any move)
  Breakeven: underlying must fall 16.47% by expiry
  RESULT: -65.3% of deployed premium. Win rate 1 of 8 (12%).
  Five of eight trades were total or near-total losses (-89% to -100%).

  Sensitivity across the entire plausible parameter grid (every cell is a loss):
    IV 45%: -34.6% / -43.8% / -56.9%  (at 20% / 35% / 60% spread)
    IV 55%: -51.3% / -58.2% / -67.9%
    IV 65%: -59.6% / -65.3% / -73.4%
    IV 85%: -66.7% / -71.4% / -78.1%
  There is no configuration of strike, tenor, IV or execution quality that rescues this. Even at an unrealistically cheap 45% IV and an unattainable 20% spread, it loses 35% of premium.

BACKTEST OF THE EQUITY SHORT (removes option decay and spread entirely — the most favorable possible expression):
  borrow 0.5%/yr: mean -23.21%, median -18.81%, 2 of 8 profitable, worst -116.8%
  borrow 3.0%/yr: mean -23.60%, median -19.21%
  borrow 10%/yr:  mean -24.72%, median -20.32%
  Borrow cost is nearly irrelevant — it moves the answer by 1.5 points across a 20x range. The loss is directional, not financing-driven. And the -117% tail is unbounded: that is the 2023-11-08 "chose not to renew its Master Repurchase Agreement" event, the purest form of the signal, after which the stock doubled.

WHY THE DAY-0 MOVE CANNOT BE HARVESTED EITHER. The flagged events do show a modest day-0 dip (mean -2.11%, median -2.84%, 75% negative, n=8). This is the only fragment of the thesis with the right sign, and it is uncapturable: 97% of filings arrive post-close and 0% intraday, so you can only trade the next open, into which that move has already gapped. And it is not distinguishable from noise — the broader samples show event-day mean |move| of 1.26% for PFSI (n=21, vs 1.23% baseline) and 1.52% for CACC (n=43, vs 1.34% baseline), i.e. exactly a random day. Against a 20-120% option spread or a 75-150bp equity round trip at the open, a 2% effect that you cannot reach is worth nothing.

HONEST UNCERTAINTY. The directional drift rests on n=8, which is small; I would not claim with confidence that the true forward drift is +23%. What I WILL claim with confidence is the disjunction, because each leg is independently measured: either the drift is positive (as observed), or it is approximately zero (as the larger n=64/n=43 event studies indicate) — and in EITHER case the cost stack guarantees a loss. For the put expression to break even at 35% spread and 65% IV, the underlying must fall 16.5% within 60 days on a signal whose measured event-day content is ~1.5%. That gap is roughly an order of magnitude. No refinement of the signal closes it.

BEST HONEST POINT ESTIMATE: -35% to -75% per trade on premium for the options expression; -20% to -25% per trade for the equity short. Expected annual P&L for a small trader running this properly: meaningfully negative, on 3-6 trades/year, with unbounded left-tail risk on the short version.
referee.confidence:
HIGH — that no exploitable edge exists in the direction specified. My confidence is tiered by how each finding was established, and the load-bearing findings are the mechanical ones, which are not estimates:

NEAR-CERTAIN (direct measurement, no modeling, large or complete samples):
- 0 of 62 warehouse/facility Item-1.01 8-Ks were filed during market hours; 97% post-close (16:01-17:01 ET), 3% pre-open. Read directly from EDGAR acceptance timestamps. This alone voids the latency premise, which was the strategy's central mechanism.
- Event-day price reaction is indistinguishable from a random day: PFSI 1.26% vs 1.23% baseline (n=21), CACC 1.52% vs 1.34% (n=43). There is no reaction to front-run.
- The options are untradeable in 4 of 5 names. UWMC 100-120% of mid with $0.50 strikes on a $1.50 stock; PFSI's 10%-OTM put has a zero bid and OI of 3; CACC has no near-dated chain at all. Live CBOE quotes, not estimates.
- Universe attrition: COOP delisted 10/1/2025; OMF has zero "warehouse" 8-K documents in 5.6 years. Two of six names cannot participate.
- Bearish trigger language is essentially absent from EDGAR: "declined to renew" 11 docs and "elected not to renew" 43 docs across ALL filers in 5.6 years, none in mortgage finance.

HIGH CONFIDENCE (documented in issuers' own words, corroborated across multiple companies):
- The sign-inversion mechanism. loanDepot and Home Point both state in filings that capacity reductions were their own decisions to cut costs against lower volume. This is a structural feature of uncommitted, non-usage-fee-bearing lines, not a company-specific quirk.

MODERATE CONFIDENCE (small sample, correctly flagged as such):
- The +23.13% mean / +18.74% median 40-day drift after capacity cuts rests on n=8. I would not bet on the magnitude, and I am NOT recommending the reverse trade. But the direction is corroborated by the mechanism above and by the 2023-11-08 +116.77% case, and — decisively — the conclusion does not depend on it. If the true drift were exactly zero, the trade still loses 35-78% of premium to spread, theta and vol premium.

COULD NOT VERIFY, STATED PLAINLY: I did not obtain live borrow rates for UWMC/RKT/PFSI/CACC/OMF (chartexchange 404'd; no current Fintel quote retrieved). I have not invented one. This does not affect the verdict: sensitivity testing shows borrow moving from 0.5% to 10% changes short P&L only from -23.2% to -24.7%. I also did not fetch the full text of the Notre Dame 8-K attention paper and have attributed no specific result to it.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY MIND: evidence of a LENDER-initiated, credit-driven line pull (not a borrower cost cut) disclosed intraday, in a name with a liquid options chain, ahead of the trade press. I searched specifically for this pattern and found essentially zero instances in 5.6 years of EDGAR. The one live stress event in the universe — UWMC's 35% collapse on 2026-08-06 — arrived as a bundled post-close earnings/capital-raise 8-K with no warehouse precursor whatsoever, after two months of filing silence.

The analyst's prior skepticism transfers exactly: as with naive FTD spikes, the naive event trigger has no power, and the only surviving variant would be a chronic, slow-moving, already-public condition that is fully reflected in stocks already down 52-87%. Recommend not proceeding.

referee.strategy: IPR Truce Tape — monitor PTAB (P-TACTS / USPTO ODP API) for joint motions to terminate an inter partes review, infer a settlement/license, and go long the small-cap patent licensor (InterDigital / Netlist / VirnetX / ParkerVision class).
referee.edge_case:
The premise is not crazy, and three things about it are genuinely true.

1. **The event is real and dated.** 35 U.S.C. §317 requires that an instituted IPR "shall be terminated with respect to any petitioner upon the joint request of the petitioner and the patent owner." A joint motion to terminate is therefore a hard, machine-readable, legally-compelled marker that a settlement exists. Unlike an FTD spike, it is not a noisy proxy — it is a near-deterministic indicator that *something* was signed.

2. **The event volume was historically non-trivial.** USPTO's own FY2025 End-of-Year Outcome Roundup (extracted directly from the PDF): 1,433 AIA petitions filed (1,361 IPR, 72 PGR); **368 petitions settled = 25% of 1,470 concluded outcomes**, split 190 pre-institution / 178 post-institution. Five-year settled-petition counts: FY21 465, FY22 339, FY23 402, FY24 387, FY25 368. By patent, 284 settled in FY25.

3. **The moves in these names are enormous when a license lands.** This is the part of the thesis that is unambiguously correct. Verified 2026 examples: Netlist (NLST) closed **+58.3%** on 5 Aug 2026 on the Samsung settlement — biggest one-day gain in five years, $897M five-year package ($239M upfront + up to $32.9M × 20 quarters + a 10M-share equity purchase). InterDigital **+15.0%** ($38.09, to $292.00) on the Amazon license. ParkerVision **+17.27%** on the Buffalo settlement, **+6.56%** on Zyxel. So the payoff distribution has a fat right tail — the thesis is not wrong that these events matter.

The steelman is therefore: *if* you could learn about a material license before the tape did, at a plausible 10-50% event move, even a handful of hits a year would be a serious return on a small book. The strategy dies not on the size of the move but on every other link in the chain.
referee.against_case:
The signal arrives after the money, is directionally ambiguous, is unsized, is free to everyone, and lives in an event universe that is currently collapsing. Six independent kill-shots, any one of which is sufficient.

**1. The docket is a lagging confirmation, not a leading indicator — and the lag is structurally guaranteed.**
§317(b) requires the settlement agreement itself be filed *before* termination, so the joint motion necessarily post-dates execution of the agreement. Meanwhile, for a US-listed licensor a material license is an Item 1.01 Form 8-K event due within four business days — and because it is *good* news, management press-releases it immediately. Live, checkable case: Netlist entered the Settlement and Release Agreement with Samsung on **4 Aug 2026**, press-released **5 Aug 2026**, stock +58.3% that day. The PTAB joint motions could not have preceded that. Same pattern on every verified example: IDCC/Amazon, PRKR/Buffalo, PRKR/Zyxel, PRKR/Hisense — all announced by company press release first. By the time the docket entry posts, 100% of the move is behind you.

**2. Adverse selection — the only "docket-first" cases are the worthless ones.**
The sole scenario where the PTAB entry precedes public disclosure is a settlement too immaterial to require an 8-K or warrant a press release. Signal-first and payoff are *inversely* selected. You are systematically harvesting the subset of events with no stock reaction by construction. This is the same structural trap as the naive FTD-spike signal: the observable is real, but it is orthogonal to (here, negatively selected on) the payoff.

**3. Termination ≠ favorable license. The base rate is bad and the direction is unknowable.**
- **52% settle pre-institution** (190/368 in FY25) — the phase where the patent owner has the *least* leverage and the petitioner has spent almost nothing. Bloomberg Law's review of 253 IPR joint motions to terminate found 128 pre-institution.
- **"Capitulation settlements" are a documented category.** Unified Patents' stated policy is to settle "in exchange for an NPE license, though never for money." A joint termination with Unified or RPX means the patent owner received **zero**. The top four IPR petitioners account for ~14% of ~5,600 IPRs.
- **The terms are sealed.** §317(b) lets any party designate the agreement business-confidential, "made available only to Federal Government agencies on written request, or to any person on a showing of good cause." So the docket tells you *that* they settled — never how much, never which way the cash flows. You cannot distinguish a $239M Samsung deal from a $0 walk-away from a covenant-not-to-sue where the licensor paid.
- **Sign-flip risk:** in a large share of PTAB matters the US-listed company is the *petitioner* (the accused infringer), not the patent owner.

**4. There is no data moat. The tape is already free and pushed to everyone daily.**
Unified Patents' **"UP Daily" is a free email** containing all new cases, recent institutions, final decisions from PTAB *plus new and recently terminated district court cases*. Unified's Portal is free. Docket Alarm sells real-time PTAB/ITC/federal alerts. USPTO's ODP PTAB API v3 (released 21 Nov 2025) "synchronizes close to real time with P-TACTS." P-TACTS is publicly searchable with no login. Law360, IPWatchdog, ip fray and StockTitan cover these same-day. Your "edge" is a free mailing list and a public REST API.

**5. The event universe is collapsing right now.** Unified Patents' Q1 2026 Patent Dispute Report: **PTAB petitions fell 64.2% YoY to 131 — a historic low; IPR petitions -66.3%.** Driver: the Stewart/Squires discretionary-denial reset (March 2025 bifurcated-briefing memo, "settled expectations" doctrine, the Nov 2025 *Motorola Solutions* Fed. Cir. decision shielding Director discretion). FY25 already showed 505 DSCO decisions with 304 denied (60%). Settlements are a derivative of petitions: at that run-rate the annual settled-petition count heads toward ~130-150, not 368. You are building a pipeline for an event stream that has lost two-thirds of its volume.

**6. Post-event reversal.** Even the pops fade. ParkerVision, after a string of settlement announcements, trades at **$0.12** with a $22M market cap. Headlines document "ParkerVision's 80% gains have evaporated." You are buying the top of a news spike in a name with no cash-generative business.
referee.who_is_on_other_side:
Depends which version of the trade you actually end up doing, and both counterparties are rational.

**Version A — you buy on the press release / opening gap (what will actually happen 95%+ of the time, since the docket lags).** Your counterparty is (i) market makers supplying liquidity into a gap they are pricing with 38-73% implied vol — they know the jump distribution better than you do; (ii) long-suffering holders and retail momentum traders taking profit into a five-year-high print; and critically (iii) **the company itself and its financing counterparties**. Small-cap licensors habitually monetize good news by issuing equity — the Netlist/Samsung package literally included a Securities Purchase Agreement for Samsung to buy 10M NLST shares, i.e. new supply created at the news. The rational seller knows the terms are confidential, the headline number is a five-year *cap* not a certainty, the quarterly payments run "based on a revenue formula and subject to adjustments and refund rights," and the historical base rate is that these pops fade. Selling you a 58% one-day print on a contingent, sealed-terms receivable is a good trade for them.

**Version B — you buy on a docket entry the company has NOT press-released.** Here your counterparty is, in effect, the issuer's own disclosure committee. Management looked at this settlement and concluded it was not material enough to require an Item 1.01 8-K or merit a press release. That decision *is* the information. Whoever sells you stock is rationally selling into a non-event that you have mistaken for a catalyst. You are paying spread and impact to take the wrong side of the issuer's materiality judgment.

There is no version of this trade where you are the informed party. That is the defining problem.
referee.frictions:
Built from live quotes pulled from the CBOE delayed-quote feed and current listings, not estimates. The strategy is long-only, so borrow is not the binding cost — spread, impact, option width and taxes are.

**Equity leg — the names split into "tradable but no edge" and "edge but untradable."**

| Name | Mkt cap | Venue | Live quote | Spread | ADV |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RMBS | ~$11B | Nasdaq | 102.07 / 102.24 | **17bp** | 1.20M sh |
| IDCC | $8.72B | NasdaqGS | ~$350 stock | ~3-9bp realistic | 343k sh |
| NLST | $1.65B | **OTCQB** (Nasdaq-delisted) | 4.92 × 4.93 | ~20bp (news-inflated liquidity) | 1.75M sh |

VirnetX has $162k of TTM revenue against -$18.9M of losses — it is a shell with a 12.5% quoted spread. ParkerVision's entire daily dollar volume is about **thirteen thousand dollars**. These are the "small-cap licensors" the thesis is built on.

**Options leg — verified live CBOE quotes, IDCC spot $351.43:**
- 21 Aug (8dte) K=350C: **bid 7.20 / ask 11.40** → $4.20 wide = **45.2% of mid**. Open interest **20 contracts**, volume **0**. IV 38.4%.
- 18 Sep (~5wk) K=350C: **bid 16.00 / ask 20.00** → **22.2% of mid**. OI 35, volume 0. IV 37.2%.
- 18 Dec K=350C: bid 37.00 / ask 41.00 → 10.3% of mid. IV 43.8%.

Break-even math on the 8-day ATM call: $4.20 spread ÷ ~0.52 delta = **$8.08, a 2.3% underlying move just to cover the round trip**, before theta; carrying three days at ~$0.58/day theta pushes the required move to roughly **3.2%**. And with OI of 20-35 contracts you will not get filled at mid — you pay the ask. Total open interest in that strike is ~$63k of premium. The options market on the single most liquid patent licensor cannot absorb a real position.

RMBS is the best case in the sector and still: 21 Aug K=100C bid 5.60 / ask 6.10 = **8.5% of mid** at IV **73%**. That 70%+ IV is itself the tell — the market already charges a fat premium for exactly the patent-event jump risk you are trying to buy.

VHC's entire option chain contains **6 contracts**. NLST returned HTTP 403 from the CBOE endpoint — I could not obtain live NLST option quotes and will not fabricate them.

**Commissions:** $0-0.005/share equity, $0.50-0.65/contract options at retail/small-fund rates. Genuinely immaterial next to a 22-45% option spread. Not the binding constraint.

**Borrow:** N/A on the long leg. If you hedged short against a licensee or sector ETF, large-cap GC is roughly 0.25-0.50%/yr. **I could not verify a current NLST borrow rate** — the only figure surfaced was 6.69% from January 2023 via a Fintel snippet, which is three years stale and I am explicitly not presenting it as current.

**Taxes — the largest single line item.** Holding periods here are days. Essentially 100% of gains are short-term capital gains, taxed as ordinary income: up to 37% federal plus state. That is a **~30-45% haircut on gross profit**, applied before any of the above is recovered.

**Operational:** USPTO explicitly reserves the right to block scrapers — P-TACTS FAQ A17: parties "generating unusually high numbers of daily P-TACTS accesses… whether generated manually or in an automated fashion, may be denied access to P-TACTS without notice." A latency-race architecture carries shutdown risk.
referee.capacity:
**Per trade.** Capacity and edge are inversely related here, which is the whole problem.

- *Where a tradable move exists* (VHC/PRKR class, $20-50M caps): at 10-20% of one day's dollar volume to keep impact near 2%, that is **$1,500-$30,000 per position**. PRKR at ~$13k/day ADV means a $5,000 order is a meaningful fraction of the tape. You cannot build a position without becoming the price.
- *Where capacity exists* (IDCC, RMBS, NLST at $8-11B / $1.65B): **$250k-$2M per trade** comfortably — but the edge is exactly zero, because the company's own press release, Law360, StockTitan, Benzinga and Yahoo disseminate the news in seconds and the stock gaps in the opening auction.
- *Via options*: capped by open interest. IDCC's front-month ATM strike carries **20-35 contracts of OI** (~$40-63k of premium). Realistic deployable size **$25-100k**, at a 22-45% spread. Effectively unusable.

**Per year.** Start from the FY25 base of 368 settled petitions (284 by patent) and filter honestly: strip pre-institution walk-aways (~52%), strip Unified/RPX-style zero-consideration capitulations, strip the majority where the patent owner is a private NPE LLC, a university, or a large operating company rather than a US-listed licensor, strip cases where the listed company is the petitioner not the owner. That leaves perhaps **5-25 petitions/year** touching a listed patent-licensing pure-play. Then apply the fatal filter — cases where the docket entry is the *first* public disclosure — and you are left with roughly **0-5 events per year**, all of them adversely selected for immateriality.

Now apply the Q1 2026 collapse: petitions -64.2% YoY to 131. Everything above shrinks by another two-thirds.

**Realistic annual deployment: $0-150k of capital across 0-5 trades.** Even granting a generous and unearned 10% gross per event, that is $0-15k/year gross, before a 1-12% spread on those specific names, before impact, before ~35% STCG. It does not pay for the entity resolution layer, the ODP poller, or a single day of an analyst's time. **This is not a capacity-constrained edge; it is a capacity-irrelevant non-edge.**
referee.decay_evidence:
**The closest documented analog decayed to zero within four months of becoming public — with published numbers.**

The Kyle Bass / Hayman Capital "dispute the patent, short the stock" trade is the same information source (PTAB docket), the same universe (small-cap patent-dependent issuers), the same premise (a PTAB event moves the stock). Its history is documented in the UCLA Law Review analysis of 21 IPR filings against 16 pharmaceutical companies, Feb-Sep 2015:
- The first challenge (Acorda) produced roughly **-11.94%** one-day abnormal return.
- Across all 21, only **3** were significantly negative at 95% confidence, while **4 were significantly positive**, and challenge #12 (Pozen, 8 Jun 2015) produced **+17.69%**.
- The authors' conclusion, verbatim: *"a trading strategy based on short-term price reactions to an IPR challenge would not have been profitable after the initial few challenges."* Explanation: *"the market has adjusted to the threat of IPR challenges."*

That is a complete decay curve — from a double-digit abnormal return to statistical noise, with sign flips, inside a single year. The peer-reviewed treatment (ScienceDirect, "Dispute the patent, short the stock: Empirical analysis of a new hedge fund strategy") covers the same episode; I could not retrieve its abstract (HTTP 403) and am not quoting figures from it.

**Who already trades or distributes it:**
- **Unified Patents "UP Daily"** — a **free** daily email carrying all new PTAB cases, institutions, final decisions, plus new and recently terminated district court cases. The termination tape is literally a free mailing list.
- **Unified Patents Portal** — free PTAB case list with filing-date sort.
- **Docket Alarm** (LexisNexis) — commercial real-time alerting across PTAB, ITC, bankruptcy and federal courts; notifies on any new filing for any watched case, party, attorney or judge.
- **Lex Machina, RPX, Patexia, PatSnap, PacerMonitor** — overlapping commercial docket analytics.
- **USPTO ODP PTAB API v3** (21 Nov 2025) — 19 new endpoints covering trial proceedings, decisions and documents, "synchronizes close to real time with P-TACTS," free.
- **Law360 (dedicated PTAB Cases feed), IPWatchdog, ip fray, Bloomberg Law** — same-day editorial coverage; ip fray and Law360 both had the Netlist/Samsung settlement immediately.
- Sell-side already models these events: William Blair's Arjun Bhatia published a $40-80M recurring-revenue estimate on the IDCC/Amazon license.

I found **no vendor selling a packaged "PTAB termination → long licensor" trading signal.** I want to be precise about what that means: it is *not* evidence of an undiscovered edge. Given that the raw feed is free, real-time, and pushed daily to every patent litigator in America, the absence of a productized trading signal is far better explained by there being nothing to sell.

**Regime decay on top of strategy decay:** petitions -64.2% YoY (Q1 2026, historic low of 131), IPRs -66.3%, institution rate down from 68% (FY21) to 50% (FY25), DSCO denials 304 of 505. The pipeline that generates the events is being shut off by the USPTO itself.
referee.net_edge_estimate:
**Honest answer: negative in the tradable bucket, and unknowable-but-almost-certainly-zero in the theoretical bucket. I did not run a docket-level backtest and I am not going to pretend otherwise.**

Decompose by which trade you actually get:

**Bucket 1 — docket entry follows the press release (≈95%+ of events).** Net expectancy is **mechanically zero before costs and strictly negative after them.** The information is fully public and fully priced within seconds; you are paying spread, impact and ~35% STCG to buy something with no informational content. Expected net: **roughly -0.5% to -3% per attempt**, being the round-trip cost in the relevant names.

**Bucket 2 — docket entry precedes disclosure (0-5 events/year).** Gross expectancy is unknown but should be near zero *by construction*, because the qualifying condition (no 8-K, no press release) is the issuer's own determination of immateriality. If you nonetheless assume an optimistic +10% gross event: subtract 1-12% round-trip spread in VHC/PRKR-class names (call it 4% mid-case), subtract ~1-3% impact at any size worth having, leaving ~+4-5% pre-tax, ~**+3% after short-term tax**. On a $10-30k position that is **$300-900 per event**, 0-5 times a year — i.e. **$0-4,500/year**, with a standard error far larger than the mean given N≤5.

**Blended realistic net: indistinguishable from zero, and negative once you charge anything for infrastructure, data engineering, entity resolution (PTAB party names → tickers), or your own time.**

Three things I explicitly **cannot** quantify and refuse to invent:
1. The **median lag in days** from settlement execution → joint motion filing → PTAB termination order. I established the *ordering* from §317(b), Form 8-K Item 1.01 timing, and the Netlist case (agreement 4 Aug 2026, press release 5 Aug 2026), but not a measured distribution across a sample. Bloomberg Law's 253-motion review reports procedural phase, not day-counts.
2. The **true conditional probability that a joint termination implies a cash-positive license to a listed patent owner.** I bounded it downward hard (52% pre-institution; documented zero-consideration capitulations; sealed terms under §317(b)) but did not compute it.
3. **Current NLST borrow** (only a stale Jan-2023 6.69% figure surfaced) and **live NLST option quotes** (CBOE returned 403).

None of those three unknowns can rescue the strategy, because the timing argument alone is dispositive: **you cannot trade ahead of a disclosure that is legally required to precede the docket entry you are watching.**
referee.barriers:
Worth separating real barriers from the illusion of one — because the *absence* of a barrier is itself the diagnosis.

**What does NOT stop a small trader (and this is the problem):**
- **Data access.** P-TACTS is publicly searchable with no login. The ODP PTAB API v3 is free and "synchronizes close to real time." Unified Patents pushes a free daily email with terminations in it. There is no gate, no cost, no credential. Anything with zero acquisition cost and universal distribution is not an edge.
- **Capital.** Positions are $1.5k-30k. No minimum.
- **Legal/compliance.** Trading on public agency dockets is clean — no MNPI issue for an outsider (unlike expert networks). Not a barrier.
- **Commissions.** Immaterial at modern rates.

**What actually stops you:**
1. **You are structurally behind the disclosure.** §317(b) plus Form 8-K Item 1.01 guarantee the company's announcement precedes or coincides with the docket entry. This is not a speed problem you can engineer around; it is the wrong ordering of events. No amount of low-latency polling fixes it.
2. **Liquidity in the only names that move.** ParkerVision trades ~$13,000/day. VirnetX quotes 5.30/5.99 — a 12.5% spread — on 27k shares. You cannot get in or out at a price resembling the print.
3. **Option markets are decorative.** IDCC front-month ATM: 45% of mid in spread, 20 contracts OI, zero volume. VHC's chain has six contracts total. There is no leveraged expression vehicle.
4. **Directional ambiguity you cannot resolve.** Terms are sealed at party request under §317(b) ("available only to Federal Government agencies… or to any person on a showing of good cause"). You are trading a binary with an unknown sign and unknown magnitude.
5. **Entity resolution is real work for no payoff.** Mapping PTAB party names (subsidiaries, holdcos, assignee-of-record mismatches) to tickers, then classifying petitioner-vs-owner role and estimating materiality, is a genuine engineering project — spent to reach an expectancy of zero.
6. **USPTO will throttle you.** P-TACTS FAQ A17: high-frequency accessors "may be denied access to P-TACTS without notice."
7. **The event stream is being turned off.** Petitions -64.2% YoY to a record-low 131 in Q1 2026 under the Stewart/Squires discretionary-denial regime. Even a working edge would be starved of events.
8. **Short-term tax treatment** removes ~30-45% of anything that survives.
referee.confidence:
**HIGH that the verdict is LIKELY-ILLUSORY. Medium on the precise magnitudes.**

**Why high on the verdict** — the core argument rests on primary sources and live market data, not inference:
- The timing kill-shot is *structural*, derived from statute and SEC rules, not from a noisy backtest: §317(b) requires the settlement agreement be filed before termination, and Form 8-K Item 1.01 requires disclosure of a material definitive agreement within four business days. The docket cannot lead. Corroborated by a live case one week old (Netlist agreement 4 Aug 2026 → press release 5 Aug 2026 → +58.3% same day) and by every other verified example (IDCC/Amazon +15.0%, PRKR/Buffalo +17.27%, PRKR/Zyxel +6.56%) — all company-announced first.
- Event counts come straight from the USPTO FY2025 Outcome Roundup PDF, which I extracted and read directly (1,433 petitions; 368 settled; 190 pre- / 178 post-institution).
- Cost-stack numbers are **live quotes**, not estimates: the CBOE feed gave IDCC 8dte ATM at bid 7.20 / ask 11.40 (45.2% of mid, OI 20, vol 0), RMBS at 8.5% of mid with IV 73%, VHC stock at 5.30/5.99 (12.5%) with a six-contract chain.
- The decay precedent is published and quantified (UCLA Law Review, 21 IPR filings, decay to insignificance with sign flips inside months).
- The free-distribution point is verified directly from Unified Patents' own page describing UP Daily.

**Why only medium on magnitudes** — and these are the honest gaps:
- **No docket-level backtest was run.** I did not compile a history of PTAB terminations, match them to listed patent owners, and measure forward returns. That is the study that would convert "likely-illusory" to a proven zero. The USPTO ODP API returned "Missing Authentication Token" (403) and the legacy endpoint 301'd, so I could not pull the proceedings history in-session.
- **No measured distribution** of the settlement-execution → joint-motion → termination-order lag. The ordering is established; the day-counts are not.
- **No computed conditional probability** that a joint termination implies a cash-positive license to a listed owner. Bounded downward, not measured.
- **Could not verify current NLST borrow** (only a stale Jan-2023 6.69% figure) or **live NLST option quotes** (CBOE 403). Both are flagged as unverified rather than estimated.
- Some quote data is delayed/consolidated (the Yahoo IDCC quote came back crossed at bid 349.76 / ask 342.51, so I disregarded it and used the CBOE feed).

**Consistency with the analyst's FTD result:** this is the same failure mode, one level deeper. With FTDs, the naive spike signal was real-but-uninformative. Here the observable is even cleaner — a legally-compelled docket entry, essentially zero false positives on "did they settle" — and it *still* fails, because being a reliable indicator of an event is worthless when (a) the event was already disclosed, (b) you cannot see its sign or size, and (c) the only cases where you see it first are the cases selected for having no economic content. Clean data is not the same thing as early, directional, or exclusive data. I would not put this on the book, and I would not fund the pipeline to test it further without first running the free version of the check — pull the ODP termination history, join to a listed-issuer map, and count how many terminations preceded their 8-K. My strong prior is a single-digit count, and that those hits had no move.

referee.strategy: Miner Curtailment Ledger — use public ERCOT curtailment/heat-event data to predict weak monthly BTC production prints at RIOT, CIFR, MARA, WULF and short (or buy puts) into the first-business-day monthly production release.
referee.edge_case:
The honest steelman has three legs, and only the first is solid.

1) The production-forecasting leg is nearly mechanical and genuinely works. BTC mined ≈ (miner operating hashrate ÷ network hashrate) × 144 blocks × 3.125 BTC × days × uptime. Network hashrate and difficulty are public and exact (TheMinerMag cites difficulty 126.98T on a 14-day avg hashrate of 913.54 EH/s). Curtailment hours are observable in near-real-time from free ERCOT dashboards, and are even visible on-chain: Hashrate Index documented block times running ~51 seconds slower than non-4CP hours during June 2025 peak-avoidance, since ~17% of global hashrate sits in Texas and full curtailment pulls ~6-7% of the global network offline. So you really can forecast the BTC count ahead of the print with good accuracy.

2) The behavioral leg: retail ownership in MARA/RIOT is enormous, and headline BTC-count numbers are the most legible datapoint in the release. A plausible story is that unsophisticated flow reacts to "production fell 12% MoM" without netting the power-credit offset.

3) The event leg: these are scheduled, pre-announced, recurring catalysts with a hard timestamp — the ideal structure for an event trade if a real conditional expectation existed.

That is the strongest version. The problem is that leg 1 forecasts the wrong variable, and legs 2 and 3 are far weaker than they look.
referee.against_case:
Five independent objections, any one of which is close to disqualifying.

1) THE SIGN IS PROBABLY BACKWARDS. Curtailment credits are not a haircut — they are a separate P&L line item recognized OUTSIDE cost of revenue on Riot's Consolidated Statements of Operations. Riot booked $10.054M of power curtailment credits in Q2 2026 and $31.077M YTD through June 30, 2026 — roughly $6,335 per BTC mined. ERCOT's 4CP program charges up to ~$50,000/MW/year in transmission costs (≈$1.25M/yr for a 25MW site, ≈$5.70/MWh spread across continuous operation), and curtailing through just four 15-minute intervals drives that toward zero. In August 2023 Riot earned $31.7M in power and demand-response credits in a single month — more than all credits received in 2022 combined. Under a fixed-price PPA, selling power back into a scarcity-priced heat event routinely beats the mining margin outright. A hot, curtailment-heavy month is frequently the most profitable kind of month a Texas miner has.

2) THE BULLISH OFFSET IS IN THE SAME PRESS RELEASE YOU ARE FADING. Riot's production update discloses power credits and all-in power cost alongside the BTC count. The April 2, 2026 update read: 1,473 BTC produced, deployed hashrate 42.5 EH/s (+26%), "total power credits were $21.0M and all-in power cost fell to 3.0c/kWh." You would be shorting into a document that carries its own hedge — and the falling-cost-per-kWh line is exactly the kind of headline the market rewards.

3) NO INFORMATIONAL ASYMMETRY. Every input is free and public: ERCOT publishes 4CP calculations and real-time grid conditions at no cost; network difficulty is on-chain; deployed hashrate is company-disclosed. This is not proprietary research, it is arithmetic on public data — and the sell side already does it (Q2 2026 consensus for Riot's BTC mined was 1,527 vs 1,587 actual). Your "surprise" is only a surprise versus a naive prior, not versus the posted consensus that already embeds the public curtailment record.

4) THE TARGET VARIABLE IS SHRINKING FAST. Riot's Q2 2026 revenue of $174.2M splits as Bitcoin Mining $113.7M, Data Center $23.2M, Engineering $37.3M — mining is ~65% and falling. Meanwhile two contracted AI leases covering 241 MW carry ~$9.8 BILLION of long-term contracted revenue. Equity value is dominated by the AI lease pipeline, not by a monthly coin count. In 2026 YTD a crypto-equity basket rose ~56% while BTC fell ~17%; WULF +85%, HUT +67%, RIOT +46%, CORZ +40%, APLD +37% against BTC ~-20%. CoinShares projects listed miners could derive 70% of revenue from AI by end-2026, up from ~30%, with AI-contracted miners at 12.3x forward sales vs 5.9x for pure-plays. Riot's Q2 net loss of $(237.2)M on $174.2M revenue was driven by BTC mark-to-market, not production volume. Your signal aims at a minority and shrinking slice of the variance while absorbing 100% of the noise.

5) THE BASKET AND THE CALENDAR ARE BOTH MIS-SPECIFIED. Of the four named tickers, only RIOT and CIFR are meaningfully ERCOT-levered. TeraWulf's campuses are Lake Mariner (New York/NYISO) and Chesapeake Data & Energy (Maryland/PJM) — ERCOT curtailment data has no mechanical bearing on WULF at all. MARA is geographically diversified across multiple US states and international sites, heavily diluting any single-ISO signal. And the assumed event does not exist as described: Riot published "First Quarter 2026 Production and Operations Updates" on April 2, 2026 — a QUARTERLY release, not monthly. Bitdeer published its January 2026 update on February 10, ten days after month-end, not the first business day. "Fade into the first-business-day monthly print" is not a well-defined uniform event across this basket.
referee.who_is_on_other_side:
The buyer of your curtailment-month dip is usually better informed than you, and rationally so.

- Crypto-equity specialist funds and the sell-side analysts who publish BTC-mined estimates. They read the same free ERCOT feed, and they model the power-credit offset because it is a disclosed line item. They buy a curtailment dip precisely because they know a heat month raises the credit line and lowers all-in c/kWh. This is not a behavioral counterparty — it is someone with a more complete model than the signal implies.

- Energy-desk and power-trading participants. Luxor Energy actively runs curtailment dispatch as a commercial service for miners (two dispatches in the first two days of June 2026 as ERCOT demand approached 80+ GW). The people executing the curtailment know its economics in real time and can express that view in the equity.

- AI/datacenter-thesis buyers. With ~$9.8B of contracted AI lease revenue at Riot alone and AI-contracted miners at 12.3x forward sales, a large and growing share of the marginal buyer simply does not care about the monthly coin count. They will absorb your supply without ever engaging your thesis.

- Index and thematic ETF flows (WGMI, BITQ and similar) plus passive rebalancing — price-insensitive, deep, and indifferent to production surprises.

- Retail momentum and dealer gamma flow in MARA/RIOT, among the largest options franchises in the mid-cap universe. This flow is noise, not a stable profit source, and it cuts both ways.

Critically, there is no identifiable structurally-disadvantaged or constrained seller here — no forced-flow counterparty of the kind that underwrites a genuine risk premium. Absent that, you are simply taking directional risk against people with the same free data and a better model of the offset.
referee.frictions:
Cost stack, with explicit flags on what I could and could not verify this session. My WebSearch budget was exhausted, so live spreads and borrow rates are ESTIMATES, not verified quotes — treat them as such.

EQUITY SHORT, 1-3 day hold:
- Bid-ask (UNVERIFIED ESTIMATE): RIOT/MARA are among the most liquid mid-caps in the market; ~1c on a $10-20 tape ≈ 5-10 bps, round trip ~10-20 bps. CIFR/WULF wider, est. ~10-30 bps round trip.
- Commissions: $0 retail equities; ~$0.003/share prime brokerage ≈ 2-4 bps.
- Borrow: I COULD NOT VERIFY current borrow fees for RIOT/MARA/CIFR/WULF in this session — do not use a made-up number. Historically these are general-collateral to modestly special, but crypto miners episodically go hard-to-borrow during squeezes. Even at 10% annualized, a 2-day hold costs only ~5 bps, so borrow is NOT the binding constraint on carry. The real borrow risk is recall/buy-in at the worst moment.
- Slippage at size: est. 5-15 bps.
- Regulatory: Rule 201 short-sale circuit breaker triggers after a 10% intraday decline — routine in these names — restricting new shorts to above-the-bid exactly when the thesis is working.
- EQUITY ROUND-TRIP TOTAL: roughly 20-50 bps.

OPTIONS (the vehicle most people would actually use):
- IV: MARA IV30 quoted in the ~95.7-105 range with IV rank 74 — top-quartile of its own trailing year. ApexVol classes MARA "Tier 3, binary exposure, defined-risk only, 1-2% position sizes, speculation not income."
- At ~100% IV, the implied 1-day move is 100 ÷ √252 ≈ 6.3%; a 1-week implied move is ~10.9%. You must clear a ~6% barrier for a 1-day event bet before any costs.
- A 1-week ATM put prices near 0.4 × S × σ × √T ≈ 5.5% of spot (~$0.83 on a $15 stock).
- Bid-ask (ESTIMATE, informed by ApexVol's "bid-ask wide outside front month" note): $0.05-0.10 on that $0.83 put = 6-12% of premium one way, 12-24% round trip. Wider still on CIFR/WULF and on any OTM strike.
- Post-event IV crush: a scheduled release reliably takes 10-25% off front-month IV regardless of direction, a pure vega loss on top of the spread.
- OPTIONS ALL-IN: you need roughly a 6%+ directional move, plus ~15-20% of premium in spread, plus the IV crush. Against a plausible signal effect size of 0-2%, this is hopeless arithmetic.

TAXES: short-term capital gains at ordinary income rates on every event; no long-term treatment is achievable on a 1-3 day hold.

THE KEY POINT ON COSTS: this is NOT primarily a "frictions eat the edge" story, and I want to be precise about that. A genuine 1% per-event edge would survive a 20-50 bps equity cost stack comfortably. The disqualifier is that the expected edge is approximately zero and plausibly negative in sign, while daily volatility of ~6% is 12-40x the transaction cost. You are not being nickel-and-dimed to death; you are taking large, uncompensated directional risk.
referee.capacity:
Liquidity is NOT the binding constraint — signal availability is.

Per-trade (ESTIMATES): MARA and RIOT can likely absorb $2-10M of notional with modest impact given very heavy ADV. CIFR and WULF are thinner, est. $1-3M. A small trader ($10k-500k) will never touch a liquidity limit in these names.

Event count is the real ceiling, and it is brutal:
- Only RIOT and CIFR carry genuine ERCOT exposure. WULF (Lake Mariner NY/NYISO, Chesapeake MD/PJM) has essentially none; MARA is diversified across many US and international grids. The tradeable universe is 2 names, not 4.
- Meaningful curtailment signal is concentrated in ERCOT summer, roughly June-September — four months, not twelve.
- Riot has consolidated to QUARTERLY production updates (Q1 2026 update published April 2, 2026), cutting its event count from 12/yr to 4/yr, of which perhaps 1-2 fall in heat season.

Realistic tradeable events: ~4-10 per year, not the ~48 the four-name monthly framing implies.

Annual capacity math: even granting a generous and unearned +50 bps net per event, 8 events × $3M = $24M of notional turnover → ~$120k/yr gross. That does not cover the data subscriptions, the hand-built event database, and the analyst time required to run it — and I do not believe the +50 bps. Realistic annual capacity before the edge is indistinguishable from noise: ~$20-50M of notional turnover producing an expected P&L statistically indistinguishable from zero, with a materially negative point estimate in curtailment-heavy months.

For a small fund this fails the most basic test: it cannot pay for its own research infrastructure even under assumptions favorable to it.
referee.decay_evidence:
The informational input is thoroughly commoditized — this is about as decayed as a data signal gets.

- Ziven (formerly bitcoinminingstock.io) sells exactly this dataset: operating and installed hashrate plus BTC production for 10+ public miners (Bitdeer 73.0, MARA 70.3, CleanSpark 38.6, Riot 37.2 EH/s as of Aug 12, 2026). Freemium: free tier, $39/month Professional, $199/month API. Any edge purchasable for $39/month is not an edge.
- Hashrate Index / Luxor publishes the Hashprice Index, pool distribution, and 4CP explainers free, and Luxor Energy commercially executes curtailment dispatch for miners.
- TheMinerMag publishes monthly public-miner production and cost analysis, sourced from SEC filings, and is cited by CoinDesk.
- ERCOT publishes 4CP calculations (archived back to 1996) and real-time grid/load conditions free and public.
- The sell side already posts BTC-mined consensus estimates (Riot Q2 2026: 1,527 consensus vs 1,587 actual — a 3.9% beat), so the naive version of this forecast is embedded in published numbers.
- The curtailment event is visible on-chain to anyone watching block times (~51s slower during June 2025 4CP hours).

Beyond commoditization, the underlying economics are actively shifting away from the thesis:
- Texas regulators are developing a rulemaking to replace 4CP with a 12CP framework on 30-minute intervals across all twelve months. That would spread the curtailment signal across the whole year and destroy the summer-concentrated seasonality the strategy depends on.
- The AI pivot is decoupling these equities from BTC production outright (2026 YTD: miner basket +56% vs BTC -17%). Cipher has rebranded — ciphermining.com now redirects to cipherdigital.com — and Riot's two AI leases carry ~$9.8B of contracted revenue against $113.7M of quarterly mining revenue.

I found NO published event study on monthly production update announcement returns, and I could not verify one exists. That absence cuts against the strategy, not for it: a decade-old, freely-observable, scheduled catalyst in heavily-covered names with no documented anomaly is more likely to have no anomaly than to have an undiscovered one.
referee.net_edge_estimate:
Point estimate: approximately ZERO, with a negative tilt in exactly the months the signal fires most strongly.

Decomposition:
- Ability to forecast the BTC count ahead of the print: genuinely high, call it R² 0.8+. This part works.
- Conditional expectation of stock return given a forecast production miss: this is where it collapses. BTC mining is ~65% of Riot's revenue and falling toward a projected ~30% sector-wide by end-2026; the residual is dominated by BTC price mark-to-market (which drove the $(237.2)M Q2 net loss), AI lease headlines, and capital-raise news. The production count plausibly explains single-digit percent of print-day variance.
- Sign conditional on CURTAILMENT specifically: I estimate this is POSITIVE, not negative — i.e. the fade loses money. A curtailment-driven miss arrives bundled with a higher power-credit line ($10.054M in Q2 2026, ~$6,335/BTC) and a lower all-in power cost headline (3.0c/kWh in the Q1 2026 update), plus avoided 4CP transmission charges of up to ~$50,000/MW/yr. That is a margin-accretive event being read as a bearish one.

Net-of-cost expectancy per event: my central estimate is -0.3% to +0.2%, and I want to be explicit that the confidence interval (roughly ±2% per event) is far wider than the point estimate. With ~4-10 genuine events per year in only two ERCOT-levered names, this is statistically unresolvable in any human timeframe: you would need on the order of hundreds of events to distinguish a 30 bps effect from zero against ~6% daily vol. At 8 events/year, that is decades of data — during which the AI pivot and the 4CP-to-12CP rulemaking will have changed the regime several times over.

I am stating plainly that the true expectancy is UNKNOWABLE to better than ±2% per event without a hand-verified, issuer-by-issuer event database that accounts for cadence changes (Riot monthly→quarterly) and variable release timing (Bitdeer at T+10, not T+1). Building that database is itself a significant project, and the honest prior on what it would find is "no effect, possibly sign-flipped."
referee.confidence:
HIGH confidence in the LIKELY-ILLUSORY verdict — but with the specific components graded separately, because they are not equally well-supported.

HIGH confidence (directly documented in primary sources this session):
- Curtailment credits are a profit offset recognized outside cost of revenue: verified in Riot's Q2 2026 release ($10.054M Q2, $31.077M YTD).
- The bullish offset appears in the same release as the BTC count: verified via the April 2, 2026 Riot update ($21.0M power credits, 3.0c/kWh all-in).
- 4CP economics make curtailment strongly accretive: verified via Hashrate Index and Miner Weekly (~$50,000/MW/yr, ~$1.25M for 25MW).
- The AI pivot has decoupled these equities from BTC production: verified via Riot's revenue split ($113.7M mining of $174.2M total; 241MW/~$9.8B AI leases) and 2026 YTD performance divergence.
- Every signal input is free public data, and the derived dataset retails for $39/month.
- Riot has moved to quarterly production updates; Bitdeer reports at T+10 — the assumed event structure is mis-specified.

MEDIUM confidence:
- The precise sign and magnitude of print-day reaction to a production miss. I found no event study and could not verify one exists. I am inferring the sign from the disclosure structure and revenue mix, which is strong reasoning but not a measured result.
- WULF's and MARA's exact site-by-site grid assignments. TeraWulf's own site names (Lake Mariner, Chesapeake Data & Energy in Maryland) support the no-ERCOT-exposure claim, but I did not get an explicit ISO confirmation from the company.

LOW confidence / EXPLICITLY UNVERIFIED — do not treat these as researched numbers:
- Live bid-ask spreads on RIOT/MARA/CIFR/WULF equities and options (my search budget was exhausted; the spread figures above are reasoned estimates).
- Current borrow fee rates for all four names. I refused to invent these.
- The ERCOT system-wide offer cap value, which I chose to describe qualitatively rather than guess.

WHY THIS STILL CLEARS THE BAR FOR A VERDICT: the disqualifying facts are structural and verified, not dependent on the unverified cost inputs. Even if borrow were free and spreads were zero, the strategy would still be shorting a margin-accretive event, using free public data already in consensus, against a revenue line that is 65% of the business and shrinking, in two names rather than four, on an event calendar that does not exist as specified.

This carries exactly the same signature as the fails-to-deliver work the analyst already did: a real and easily-measured public data series, a mechanically true intermediate relationship (curtailment really does reduce the coin count, just as FTD spikes really do occur), and no surviving link from that to tradeable stock returns. The naive version is not merely unprofitable — it is pointed the wrong way.

RECOMMENDATION: do not allocate. If the analyst wants to salvage anything here, the only version worth testing is the inverse — whether heavy-curtailment months systematically produce BULLISH margin surprises via the power-credit line — and even that should be tested on RIOT and CIFR only, on a hand-verified release-date database, before a dollar is risked.

verdictSummary.strategy: Chronic-Fail Decay: systematically short (or avoid) cheap single names that appear on >=11 of the last ~13 semi-monthly SEC FTD prints, sized by price band, held ~2 weeks. Universe ~650-730 names/print, median price ~$1.93, dominated by optionable busted-growth names (PLUG, BYND, CGC, SPCE, HYZN, GETY, VUZI, LAES, VFS, FBIO).
verdictSummary.verdict: NO-EDGE (as a short strategy). The statistical pattern is real and was published a decade ago; the exploitable net-of-cost expectancy is negative with high confidence. The only surviving use is as a free long-side negative screen.
verdictSummary.confidence:
HIGH that no exploitable short edge exists; MEDIUM-HIGH on the precise magnitude of the loss.

Reasons for high confidence: (1) The two decisive numbers come from the commissioning analyst's own data, not from my research — a +1.56% mean and a -0.21% lag-honest median. A fixed-dollar short earns the negative of the mean; that is arithmetic, not opinion, and it means the strategy has negative expectancy BEFORE any cost I researched. (2) The spread floor is a regulatory constant (SEC Rule 612: $0.01 above $1.00, $0.005 only for demonstrably tight names) and at a $1.93 median price it is 0.52% per round trip, more than double the honest signal. (3) Borrow rates are verified primary-source observations from Interactive Brokers for six of the ten named chronic stocks, and they are inversely aligned with the edge in exactly the way Muravyev-Pearson-Pollet predict. (4) The result is already published (Stratmann & Welborn 2016, same dataset), already factor-spanned (Drechsler CME factor, Bali MAX, Asness QMJ), already commercialized by multiple vendors, and the underlying state is disseminated free and daily via the Reg SHO threshold list. (5) The JF 2025 paper is a direct, out-of-sample, general refutation: 162 anomalies go from +0.14%/mo gross to -0.01%/mo net of borrow, and are unprofitable even gross once the high-fee 12% is removed. This strategy is entirely inside that high-fee 12%. (6) Three independent kill mechanisms — negative gross mean, cost floor exceeding the signal, and the edge being the borrow fee itself — each sufficient alone; all three would have to be wrong simultaneously.

Reasons the magnitude estimate is only medium-high: I could not obtain live NBBO spreads (used tick-size floors, which understate cost), could not obtain historical or cohort-wide borrow distributions (six point observations plus literature deciles), could not verify BYND's current short-interest percentage of float (source returned 403), and the 234% IV figure is single-sourced. Every one of these gaps, if resolved, makes the trade WORSE, not better — my estimate is biased in the strategy's favor and it still fails.

The single most important thing I would tell the analyst: you did not discover an FTD anomaly, you rediscovered the securities-lending fee. The signal ranks names by how expensive they are to borrow, and the lender charges you the entire spread. If you want to test whether anything is left, do not run a short book — measure the MEAN (not the median) of the market-neutral chronic-minus-fresh spread, and regress the chronic-minus-fresh return on the contemporaneous borrow fee. If the alpha vanishes when you control for the fee, which I expect, the question is closed.

verdictSummary.strategy: Reg SHO Threshold-List Overvaluation Reversal — short (or buy puts on) names newly added to / persisting on SRO Reg SHO threshold lists, per Autore, Boulton & Braga-Alves (2015), Financial Review 50(2), 143-172.
verdictSummary.confidence:
HIGH that there is no exploitable net edge for a small trader or small fund. Medium-high on the precise magnitude of the gross pattern.

WHY HIGH: the conclusion does not rest on the return estimate at all. It rests on two independently verified facts that cannot be argued around. First, 8 of the 20 highest-borrow-fee stocks in the entire US market sit on today's 74-name threshold list at 756-1,074%/yr — a 31x concentration versus random — which means a 30-day hold costs 63-88% of notional against a 19-21% gross median. Second, the most liquid optionable name on the list, HTZ, prices a 22-day ATM put at 20.2% of spot against a 20.3% median 21-day decline, i.e. the options market has already fully priced the effect. Both are direct measurements from live market data taken today, not estimates. Additionally the paper's own authors state the mispricing "is likely to be difficult to arbitrage because of extreme shorting costs" — they never claimed it was tradeable.

WHY NOT HIGHER ON THE GROSS MAGNITUDE — things I could NOT verify, stated plainly:
- The IBKR borrow fees came from chartexchange's screener with NO visible timestamp. I could not reach IBKR's own securities-lending file from this environment (both the FTP and https endpoints returned nothing). The 8/20 overlap is so extreme it is robust to staleness, but treat the individual percentages as indicative rather than executable quotes.
- Cboe quotes were captured after the close (last trade 2026-08-12 16:00), so spreads may be wider than mid-session. I have flagged them as an upper bound; intraday spreads on the common names are likely somewhat tighter than the 4.28% median.
- Put-call-parity implied borrow assumes European-style parity on American options with no dividends. Early exercise on hard-to-borrow names biases this; treat 25-88%/yr as an order-of-magnitude estimate.
- I used ONLY the Nasdaq threshold list. NYSE, Cboe and the FINRA OTC lists are not included; the OTC list in particular is larger and would be strictly worse on every friction.
- I have no shares-outstanding data, so I could not reconstruct threshold membership before 2023-01-03. The 3.5-year window covers 879 trading days and ~47 independent monthly observations — adequate but not long.
- Prices are the FTD file's embedded prior-day closes, unadjusted for splits. I applied a +/-70% one-day guard at entry, but reverse splits inside the forward window remain and bias short returns DOWNWARD (making my gross figures conservative).
- Returns condition on the name reappearing in the FTD file later. Delistings-to-zero drop out, which biases short returns DOWNWARD too. So the true gross is if anything better than I report — and the net conclusion is unaffected, because the borrow fee is 3x the gross either way.

RECOMMENDATION: reject as a trade. Adopt the on-threshold-list flag as a free do-not-own screen alongside the existing chronic-FTD filter, and route the research effort elsewhere. If anyone wants exposure to this phenomenon, the economically correct expression is to be the LENDER, not the short — but that requires a prime brokerage balance sheet, not a trading account.

verdictSummary.strategy: FTD-Confirmed Short-Constraint Long-Short — use SEC fails-to-deliver (chronic-persistence + low-price pattern) as a confirming filter on a high-borrow-fee / high-utilization / high-days-to-cover short-constraint anomaly, traded by a small trader or small fund.
verdictSummary.confidence:
HIGH — unusually so, because this rests on a reproduced computational finding rather than only on judgment.

verdictSummary.confidence:
HIGH — and higher than I am normally willing to be on a rejection, for three specific reasons.

1. THE CORE RESULT IS ALGEBRAIC, NOT STATISTICAL. It requires no backtest, no sample period, and no distributional assumption. An options-hedged lender earns rf − borrow × (1 − split × util). For any positive borrow fee and any split below 100%, that is strictly less than rf. There is no parameter choice — no borrow fee, no utilization rate, no volatility regime — that flips the sign. This is not "the edge is probably too small"; it is "the edge has the wrong sign by construction." I stress-tested it at 50% and 60% splits and at 25%, 50% and 100% utilization; all nine combinations lose to T-bills before costs.

2. THE FACTUAL PREMISE IS DIRECTLY FALSIFIED BY OBSERVED DATA, NOT INFERENCE. The strategy is predicated on XRT being persistently hard to borrow with a high sustained fee. The measured fee is 1.07% with 500,000 shares freely available (ChartExchange/IBKR, 2026-08-12). Even at the peak of the 2021 meme-stock episode, S3's Ihor Dusaniwsky publicly noted XRT at 2.32% — cheaper to short than GME at 1.70%. The premise is not merely optimistic; it is inverted, and the academic literature explains why: XRT is the "short favorite" that intermediates most shorting AT LOW FEES, which is exactly why its short interest is 568% of float.

3. I VERIFIED THE HEDGE-PRICING CLAIM EMPIRICALLY RATHER THAN ASSUMING IT. Rather than asserting that options price the borrow, I pulled live CBOE quotes and inverted put-call parity across every liquid strike with a proper dividend schedule. Implied borrow came out at 0.79%, 1.11%, 1.43% and 1.57% against a 1.07% quoted cash fee. The options market has it right to within the bid-ask. That closes the only loophole through which this trade could have worked.

CALIBRATION AND WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY MIND. My confidence is in the VERDICT, not in every input. Three numbers I could not verify and have flagged rather than fabricated: XRT-specific realized SYEP utilization (no broker publishes it; IBKR's own pages returned HTTP 403 to every fetch attempt, so all IBKR program terms here come from secondary sources and IBKR's own guides subdomain rather than the primary pricing page); IBKR's wholesale lending rate versus the 1.07% retail short charge; and the paywalled long-run XRT fee history. Critically, all three uncertainties push the conclusion in the SAME direction — the wholesale rate is typically below the retail short charge, and lower utilization means less income — so resolving them can only make the trade worse.

I would revisit only on a genuinely different setup: a lender split above 100% (does not exist), an ETF where option-implied borrow sits materially BELOW the achievable lending rate (I found the opposite), or AP status enabling real create-to-lend with full fee capture and redemption optionality. None is available to a small trader. This same failure mode — a dramatic surface statistic (568% short interest) that is a mechanical artifact rather than evidence of scarcity — is precisely the pattern the analyst's FTD work already identified. Recommend declining without further work.

verdictSummary.strategy: Illiquid-Underlying ETF NAV-Discount Convergence — buying HY/muni/bank-loan/EM bond ETFs when they trade at a wide, persistent discount to NAV during market stress, on the thesis that APs will eventually arbitrage the gap closed (March 2020 as case study).
verdictSummary.confidence:
HIGH that the verdict is LIKELY-ILLUSORY, for a small trader or small fund.

Reasons for high confidence: (a) The direct empirical test is unambiguous and I computed it myself from raw price data — 95% of identifiable wide-discount entries lost money over 5 days, averaging -7.88%, in the single most favorable episode that has ever existed for this trade. A strategy that fails on its own best case study does not require further testing. (b) The structural barriers (no create/redeem, no way to short NAV) are absolute, not matters of degree, and they are independent of any statistical question. (c) The cost stack alone kills it: I verified live option quotes of 12-30% of mid on HYG and 30-200% on LQD, versus an average crisis signal of 1.0-1.4%, using BlackRock's own numbers. (d) The revealed preference of the APs — the only parties who could do the real arbitrage, who had every incentive, and who passed for two weeks — independently confirms the discount was compensation for risk rather than mispricing. Four independent lines of evidence converge on the same answer.

Reasons it is not stated as certainty: (a) My forward-return test is effectively one event across correlated instruments; overlapping windows on five funds in one crisis is closer to n=1 than n=30, and I have not run a multi-decade panel of daily premium/discount data — I attempted to obtain iShares' historical premium/discount series and the SEC/BIS underlying data and could not retrieve machine-readable history. (b) I could not verify March 2020 borrow rates, March 2020 option bid-ask widths, or the VXHYG implied-vol path (the index returned no time series), so the hedge cost is inferred from realized vol (50-58% annualized) rather than from observed IV prints. (c) I could not verify April 2025 tariff-shock discount magnitudes, which would be the cleanest test of decay.

Notably, every one of these gaps concerns evidence that would make the strategy look WORSE, not better — stressed borrow and stressed option spreads are strictly higher than the calm-market figures I used, so my cost stack is conservative. The verdict would only flip on evidence that discounts systematically predict positive risk-adjusted forward returns at identifiable entries, and I found the opposite.

I would upgrade to NO-EDGE if given a full daily premium/discount panel confirming no predictive power out of sample; the reason I stop at LIKELY-ILLUSORY is that a genuine liquidity risk premium does exist here — it is simply earned by balance sheet, and unavailable to the trader in question.

verdictSummary.strategy: Daily Short-Volume Reversal using FINRA's free daily short-sale volume file (short heavily short-sold names, buy lightly short-sold names), gated by an SEC fails-to-deliver (FTD) filter, motivated by Diether–Lee–Werner (2009, RFS 22:2).
verdictSummary.confidence:
HIGH that there is no exploitable net-of-cost edge here for a small trader or small fund, for four converging reasons that do not depend on each other.

(a) The originating paper's own cost arithmetic is negative: 1.39%/month gross versus 2.7%/month execution cost, stated by DLW in the published text, in the best-case 2005 sample, on price>=$5 stocks, using exchange-marked tick data superior to anything public today.
(b) The specific horizon this strategy trades has a direct, peer-reviewed null result in the public-data era — Wang-Yan-Zheng (JFE 2020): "abnormal short-term shorting flows do not predict future returns or anticipate bad news."
(c) My own measurement of the current file shows the cross-sectional dispersion that a sort would exploit is a liquidity artifact — ratio IQR falls monotonically from 0.661 in sub-1k-share names to 0.171 in >10M-share names, 75.6% of variance is within-name daily noise, and the extreme deciles have ~1/12th the volume of the median name.
(d) The gate makes it worse, not better: only ~5 names/day pass both filters, at median $1.47/share where the 170% margin rule, Rule 201, absent options, and deep-special borrow all apply simultaneously.

MEDIUM on the precise magnitude of the negative expectancy, because I could not run an independent return backtest (no free price feed reachable through the proxy) and could not verify current per-name borrow fees or per-market-cap effective spreads with an authoritative source. My spread figures lean on a 2014 SEC study of 2013 data, and my borrow-fee framing leans on D'Avolio (2002) plus a vendor aggregate whose methodology I could not check. Those uncertainties affect how negative the answer is, not its sign.

LOW confidence only on one sub-question: whether the correct sign is negative or actively inverted. SqueezeMetrics' commercial DIX product asserts high short volume proxies BUYING, with intraday returns uniformly positive above a 35% ratio — but that is a vendor white paper, not peer-reviewed, and I did not independently verify it. Either way it argues against the trade as specified; it just changes whether the strategy is dead or backwards.

Recommendation: do not put this on the book. If any variant is worth further work, it is the slow one Wang-Yan-Zheng actually validated — long-horizon accumulated shorting flow with a one-year decay — which is a low-turnover signal in liquid names, is essentially a proxy for short interest, and is already sold by multiple vendors. The daily-reversal-plus-FTD-gate construction should be retired for the same reason the analyst retired naive FTD spikes: it is a sort on noise in names too small to trade.

verdictSummary.strategy: Section 103(k) Coal Tripwire — monitor MSHA Section 103(k) accident/control orders on msha.gov and short the affected US-listed coal issuer (HCC, AMR, BTU, METC) into the expected production disruption.
verdictSummary.confidence: HIGH — and unusually so for a rejection, because this was settled by direct measurement rather than by argument. I downloaded and parsed the complete MSHA violations census (3,092,333 rows, file dated 2026-08-07), isolated all 14,142 Section 103(k) orders since 2000, mapped 324 of them to mines controlled by HCC/AMR/BTU/METC since 2019, and ran the event study against XME-adjusted daily returns. The decisive facts are measurements, not inferences: issue-day relative volume 0.87-1.12x, issue-day |return| at or below unconditional baseline for two of four names, full-sample drift wrong-signed at +2.40% over five days, post-2021 drift +0.07%. Publication latency is verified from the file itself (weekly Friday refresh, 84 rows on the most recent weekday vs a ~300-600/day steady state, zero rows on the file date). Borrow fees and option quotes are live vendor data, not estimates. Two independent peer-reviewed studies concur, and the Long View / Centurion case studies show the material events are either private-company or non-MSHA. Residual uncertainties, stated plainly: (a) equity bid-ask is a Corwin-Schultz proxy, not a live NBBO quote — it is the softest number in the stack, though even a 5bp spread does not rescue a zero-to-negative gross signal; (b) ScienceDirect returned 403, so the 155bp/140bp Christensen et al. figure comes from a search-result summary of the article page and is not verified from the paper itself — the 2021 Resources Policy finding is likewise from summary, though it is directionally corroborated by my own measurement; (c) the concentrated sub-case (mine-wide 103(k) at a mine >40% of volumes) is under-powered at N=27 and I label its expectancy unknowable rather than zero. None of those caveats moves the verdict. This is the same failure mode as the naive FTD spike signal: a real, well-documented public dataset with a plausible causal story, no abnormal volume or return at the event, and a positive-looking t-statistic that dissolves into calendar clustering the moment you cut it by year. The chronic-persistence lesson applies here too — if anything survives in MSHA data it will be a slow, structural, cross-sectional quality signal (chronic violation intensity as a proxy for operational deterioration or cost inflation, held over quarters), not a same-week event tripwire.
